World.title: Burnham will divert ‘significant’ resources out of civil service, says No. 10 North chief
World.content:
Burnham’s Cabinet signed a statement last month which said No. 10 North would oversee a “major transfer of powers, resources and functions” from central to local government before the next general election, due by 2029. It promised to “build new career paths between central government and the wider public sector” and make the civil service “smaller and more strategic.”

Britain’s civil service has ballooned by 100,000 people in six years to around 550,000 following the Covid-19 pandemic and the U.K.’s exit from the European Union.

Simpson declined to say to what extent the overall headcount of civil servants will be cut to increase staffing in regional government. “I am not going to put a figure on what that is going to look like,” she said.

However, she added: “The intent behind [the Cabinet paper] — really moving significant resource from Whitehall and from the civil service into regions, into local areas — is absolutely part of our plan, our ambition, our mission here in No. 10 North.”

Burnham has said he wants all areas of England to have mayoral authorities in place by the end of 2028, and they are set to be offered the expertise of Whitehall officials where it is relevant and desired.

It is not yet clear how this movement of staff will work in practice. Officials plan to outline more detail in a paper alongside the Oct. 26 budget, which — as with a spending review in 2027 — will make clear the impact on Whitehall budgets.

World.title: The drone war is coming for global shipping
World.content:
But the novel attacks are also opening a phase of geopolitical crisis where merchant vessels at large are facing the risk of drone attacks. That, in turn, risks causing a maritime arms race.

A remarkable chain of events began in early July: Ukrainian drones started hitting Russian-linked merchant vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov on an almost daily basis. They had struck the occasional shadow vessel in the Mediterranean or Russian oil installations and oil terminals before that, but this campaign was different; several ships were being struck each day.

The culmination was a remarkable 172 ships hit in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov within the course of just 12 days. In fact, Ukraine reported attacks on 15 Russian shadow vessels, including seven tankers and five dry cargo ships, over the course of one night alone.

These attacks then continued, with Ukraine attacking all manner of Russian-linked ships — primarily tankers but others too. In truth, some of the targets have not been shadow vessels, as the illegal fleet primarily operates in the Baltic Sea where ships carrying Russian oil above the price cap traverse to reach their destinations. In the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, far from the Western coastal countries that have imposed the price cap, Russian cargo doesn’t require such workarounds. (These vessels, though, still serve Moscow’s war effort, transporting goods to Crimea and other Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.)

Named MoLoCHKa — a Ukrainian acronym that translates to “Moscow will fall because of Crimea” — the Ukrainian military’s campaign against Russian-linked shipping has been a rude awakening for Moscow, which has had to move drone units from other duties to protect merchant shipping instead.

According to Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Commander, Robert Brovdi, Moscow has had to deploy up to 200 drone-operator groups to ship-protection duties. It has also begun equipping oil tankers with anti-drone technology, reported the Financial Times.

World.title: There’ll be some ups and downs: The politics of theme parks
World.content:
Anyway, there are also links between theme parks and politics — and not just because spending too long doing either can make you vomit.

Earlier this month, French President Emmanuel Macron sought Saudi investment to turn what was once the country’s biggest theme park into a manga-themed attraction. The site used to be home to Mirapolis, which celebrated French literature and culture (“c’mon kids, let’s go ride a rollercoaster based on Proust’s ‘À la recherche du temps perdu.’ The queues are short, but the ride lasts 200 hours”) but closed down in 1991 due to financial difficulties.

Then there’s the Puy du Fou theme park, which has one location in France and one in Spain, and now wants to open another in the U.K. Philippe de Villiers, its founder and president, has been linked with Russian President Vladimir Putin and previously proposed the construction of a theme park in Crimea after Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014.

Next comes Thierry Breton, the former European Commissioner for the Internal Market and Getting Into Fights With Elon Musk, who helped come up with the idea for a high-tech theme park called “Futuroscope,” just north of Poitiers in western France. Its tagline is: “Expect the unexpected,” which was very much the theme of Breton’s time in Brussels.

Theme parks aren’t just occasionally political though; they can also be weird.

There’s Wunderland Kalkar in Germany, which is on the site of a former nuclear power plant — one that was never operational, as the entire project was abandoned due to safety concerns. There’s South Korea’s Loveland, an adult-only sculpture park that features explicit artwork (maybe President Donald Trump found out about it just before cooling diplomatic ties with Seoul). And then there’s Colombia’s Parques Temáticos Hacienda Nápoles, a theme park on the grounds of former drug baron Pablo Escobar’s ranch (sounds like a wild ride).

World.title: Sánchez has one year until Spain’s election deadline. The odds are against him.
World.content:
Spain's Prime Minister gestures as he addresses journalists after meeting King Felipe VI of Spain at the Almudaina Palace in Palma de Mallorca, Spain on July 29, 2026. | Jaime Reina/ AFP via Getty Images

The prime minister is still facing heat over the Ceuta crisis and a raft of Socialist Party corruption scandals. An early election could make sense.

We are now one year away from the latest possible date — Aug. 22, 2027 — that Spain can hold a general election.

For embattled Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, it looks like it’s going to be a bruising ride to get that far. He insists he will seek reelection, brushing aside the predictions that he is doomed by pointing to his well-established knack for defying political gravity.

But this time, the odds are especially stacked against him and his fragile minority government, which has never appeared so isolated.



The challenges that lie ahead are so daunting that Sánchez could well chuck the schedule and call for an early vote.

Here’s why he’s up against it.

Rough rentrée

Summers have historically been kind to Sánchez.

In the past, the seasonal break helped reduce the heat generated by crises like the June 2025 arrest of high-ranking Socialist Party official Santos Cerdán for allegedly awarding public works contracts in exchange for kickbacks. The prime minister was no doubt hoping a similar scenario would play out following this spring’s high-profile indictment of his ally, former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, on money-laundering charges, and after a major raid on his party’s headquarters as part of a separate criminal investigation.

But just days before he was due to head off on a beach break on the island of Lanzarote, Sánchez’s summer was upended by a surge of 72,000 migrants into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in northern Africa. Even though the prime minister did eventually resume his scheduled vacation, the Ceuta crisis has continued to dominate the news. Thousands of unauthorized migrants remain in the city, with local authorities complaining Madrid isn’t doing enough to address overwhelmed hospitals and other public services.

Migrants wait to receive water on the beach next to the CETI (Centros de Estancia Temporal de Inmigrantes) on August 2, 2026 in Ceuta, Spain. | Adri Salido/Getty Images

The government is bound to face tough grillings over security failures, whether intelligence warnings went unheeded and whether something went badly wrong in relations with Morocco. The Ceuta debacle also left Sánchez looking painfully isolated on the EU stage, with 22 leaders writing a letter suggesting his liberal migration policies could have helped attract the influx.

Nearly a third of Sánchez’s ministers have been summoned to testify at extraordinary hearings in the Spanish parliament next week, and the prime minister himself is due to face tough questions when plenary sessions resume in September.

So much for a fresh start.

Budget bloodbath

The fall promises no relief for Spain’s prime minister, who faces defeat in a battle over the national cashflow.

The minority government has been unable to pass a single budget bill during this legislative term, and has been operating on the spending plan approved by Sánchez’s previous government in December 2022. The Socialist leader has vowed to submit a draft budget for 2027 this fall, but it is almost certain to be rejected by lawmakers.



A major obstacle is the Catalan separatist Together for Catalonia group, whose support is key to getting any legislation passed. The party voted down the deficit framework for the draft budget this summer, with its spokesperson, Josep Rius, characterizing the long-shot legislation as “yet another Sánchez frivolity.”

The separatists were instrumental in getting Sánchez a third stint as prime minister in 2023, but relations have since soured, with the party now accusing the government of reneging on its commitments to Catalonia, and refusing to back budget plans it considers to be Madrid-centric.

But the prime minister is determined to move forward, raising questions about his motivation to present a doomed budget bill.

“There’s growing speculation that Sánchez may want to call voters to the polls as early as March, and the budget’s failure would provide him with an excuse to do so” said Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University, who pointed out that Spain is due to hold local and key regional elections in May 2027.



Sánchez’s personal unpopularity has been cited as a key factor in Socialist Party losses in previous local and regional races. Holding national elections earlier in the year could remove the prime minister from the equation when the May vote is held, helping center-left candidates running in key cities and enabling the socialists retain control of regional governments in Castilla-La Mancha, Asturias and Navarre.

“There’s no sense in stretching this term to its limits if you’re not only going to lose, but drag others down with you,” Simón said.

(More) legal woes ahead

Sánchez’s tumultuous relationship with Spain’s judiciary is also likely to grow even more strained over the next year.

In the coming months the prime minister’s wife, Begoña Gómez, could stand trial on charges of influence-peddling and embezzlement. She denies all wrongdoing, and the prime minister has consistently argued that his wife is the victim of so-called “lawfare” targeting his friends and family.

Spain’s prime minister sits with his wife Begona Gómez as they attend the 41st congress of the Spanish Socialist Workers Party (PSOE) at the Palacio de Exposiciones in Seville, on December 1, 2024. | Cristina QuiclerAFP via Getty Images

Gómez’s trial follows on this summer’s conviction of the prime minister’s brother on administrative misconduct charges, in connection to the rigged allocation of a public job — a ruling Sánchez called “unjust.”

Beyond the cases involving his immediate family, the prime minister faces potentially damaging judicial probes into alleged bid-rigging and kickbacks involving key allies — as well as an explosive investigation into suspected illegal financing of his Socialist Party.

Crucial parliamentary allies such as Gabriel Rufián of the Republican Left of Catalonia have warned that illegal financing is a “red line.” Hard evidence could force Spain’s current prime minister to suffer the same fate as his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy, whom Sánchez ousted from power after his People’s Party was proven to have engaged in the same crime.

Left-wing logjam

Spain’s fragmented politics make majority governments increasingly unlikely: Power goes to whoever can secure enough parliamentary support to be declared prime minister.

For now, the polling suggests the center-right People’s Party and the far-right Vox party are on course to control a majority of seats in the parliament in 2027. The two parties currently govern in coalition in four Spanish regions, and PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo in June explicitly endorsed a partnership at the national level.

Sánchez faces tougher odds in building an alliance strong enough to keep him in power. In 2023, he formed a coalition with the Sumar group — an amalgam of far-left parties — and won the backing of key regionalist and separatist parties.

But this time around, the numbers don’t add up. Sumar has effectively collapsed amid internal infighting, and its unifying leader, Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz, has ruled out standing as its candidate at the next election. Polls indicate the far left will suffer heavy losses at the national level, leaving Sánchez with fewer viable paths to a parliamentary majority.

No relief abroad

There are also signs that Sánchez will no longer be able to boost his fortunes at home through his performances on the global stage.

Engagement in international affairs — ranging from his condemnation of Israel’s military operations in Gaza, to his ongoing feud with U.S. President Donald Trump — has previously bolstered his standing in Spain.

But political scientist Simón said that the harsh criticism the prime minister from fellow EU leaders for his handling of the Ceuta crisis reveals he is increasingly considered to be a figure on his way out.



“As one of the few social democrats still governing in Europe, his positions are out of step with the conservative consensus, and they aren’t taken seriously because he is now seen as a lame duck who is going to lose the next elections,” said Simón.

“That leaves him with little capacity to make a difference because he isn’t seen as representing Spain’s position at this point,” he added. “Everyone accepts someone else will be in charge next year, and likely have a very different perspective.”

Sánchez’s broader international vulnerabilities will be on display in November, when Madrid hosts a summit of Ibero-American heads of government that will underscore the region’s rightward shift. Roughly half the leaders attending are from the right, and include figures like Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, with whom the prime minister has a prickly relationship.

“The summit highlights a global political realignment,” said Simón. “One that Spain narrowly avoided in 2023, but seems increasingly inevitable next year.”

World.title: En brandissant la carte Breton, Bayrou fâche les bayrouistes
World.content:
Poulain et lévriers

“ Ce choix n’a aucun sens, Thierry Breton n’incarne pas le changement, mais l’establishment européen et industriel. Et il ne respire pas l’empathie avec les gens ”, lâche encore, franchement en colère, un autre compagnon de route. “ Sans prévenir, Bayrou nous a sorti ce nom de derrière les fagots. Il n’y a pas un mec qui suit ”, renchérit un parlementaire, persuadé que Breton n’est agité que comme un leurre par l’ancien Premier ministre. “C’est comme dans les courses de lévriers, il y en a toujours en carton devant ! ”

Comprenez : Bayrou, qui n’entend soutenir ni Gabriel Attal ni Edouard Philippe, avec lesquels ses rapports sont dégradés, et n’est pas en position de se présenter lui-même, ne chercherait qu’à gagner du temps en défendant un autre poulain. Avant, éventuellement, de jouer “les faiseurs de roi”, comme en 2017 lorsqu’il s’était rallié à Emmanuel Macron.

Le 9 août, les lieutenants de Bayrou ont aussi eu la surprise de découvrir que l’ancien Premier ministre avait décidé de plaider publiquement en faveur l’organisation d’une primaire allant des socialistes aux “gaullistes ” — idée jusque-là jamais développée par l’intéressé.

A défaut, donc, Bayrou prône la mise en orbite d’une personnalité rassembleuse… comme Thierry Breton, cité en premier parmi les candidats potentiels à ses yeux. Et de faire l’éloge de cet homme “enraciné dans la grande famille démocrate et réformatrice”, qui n’a pas “ appartenu au pouvoir sortant” — rappelons tout de même qu’il doit sa nomination comme commissaire européen à Emmanuel Macron — avec “une capacité à réunir très largement”. Thierry Breton serait le “seul” responsable européen à avoir ”résisté à Donald Trump et à Vladimir Poutine”, assure encore Bayrou.

Bayrou insiste

Déconnexion liée aux vacances, ou gêne ? Les piliers du parti (Jean-No¨ël Barrot, Marc Fesneau, Sarah El Haïry…) n’ont pas relayé ou commenté l’interview de leur patron sur X.

Joint ce jeudi par téléphone, l’ancien Premier ministre persiste et signe : “Face au risque d’un duel mortel pour le pays entre Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon au second tour, et face au risque d’une crise financière qui peut être imminente, avec l’explosion de la charge de la dette, avant ou aussitôt après l’élection, il faut qu’apparaissent des visages nouveaux capables de renouveler ou de fédérer des forces qui acceptent, le moment venu, de se regrouper autour d’elles.”

World.title: Romanian jet blasts drone near offshore gas platform, president blames Moscow
World.content:
“I strongly condemn the intensification of these types of irresponsible incidents on the part of the Russian Federation,” he wrote in a post on X.

European Commission President Von der Leyen also weighed in on the incident, lending European solidarity to Romania. “An escalating campaign of threats is underway, unsettling our citizens and seeking to divide our Union,” she wrote on X.

“With the European Drone Defence Initiative and the Eastern Flank Watch, we are scaling up production in Europe ... So we can respond to emerging threats with speed, unity and resolve.”

According to a Facebook post by Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruță, the drone was spotted by Romania’s Coast Guard a few hundred meters from the Neptun Deep platform, where several hundred people were working. After consulting the president, Romanian authorities scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and ordered the drone be destroyed.

Miruță said the drone had not come from its neighbor: “Through the direct communication channel recently created with the Ukrainian side, I received the official confirmation that it is not of Ukrainian origin.”

Neptun Deep is Romania’s largest natural gas development and is located in the Black Sea. Romania began developing the project in 2023, with the first gas to be extracted in 2027; it is expected to help Romania become the EU’s largest producer of natural gas.

NATO allies have previously raised concerns about protecting Neptun Deep from Russian drone attacks. Von der Leyen called the incident “hybrid warfare.”

The Russian embassy in Romania did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Spain moves hundreds of migrants from Ceuta beach to temporary shelters
World.content:
National Police and Civil Guard officers escorted migrants to temporary reception sites at Loma Margarita and El Embolsamiento. More than 1,200 people had been transferred by late morning, while local reports put the total at up to 1,700. The beach was later cleared, although some migrants returned.

 

Spain has prepared space for around 1,800 people in military facilities and tents, with further sites due to open in the coming days. The centres are intended to provide water, food, toilets, psychosocial support and safer accommodation, while restoring sanitary conditions on the beach.

The UN refugee agency has urged Spain to guarantee access to healthcare and asylum procedures and to identify people in need of international protection. Human Rights Watch said on 21 August that thousands had spent almost three weeks sleeping outdoors without adequate sanitation or clear access to legal procedures.

The crisis followed a mass arrival from Morocco on 30 and 31 July, when more than 72,000 people reached Ceuta, according to Spanish government estimates. Most have since returned to Morocco, but at least 90 people were reported to have died during the surge.

World.title: Russian drones hit border crossing with Moldova in overnight strike, Ukraine says
World.content:
A border crossing with Moldova in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region was damaged by Russian drones overnight, the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine said in a statement on Friday morning.

 

Traffic through the Tabaky checkpoint has been suspended and diverted to other crossings, the border service said on Telegram.

Moldovan authorities in Chișinău have been informed, the statement added.

The announcement comes a day after a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed an explosive-laden maritime drone close to Europe's largest offshore gas project, hours after another drone entered the NATO member's airspace and crashed near the Ukrainian border.

Romania's President Nicuşor Dan blamed Russia for the latest incident and condemned what he called an escalation of "irresponsible incidents" by Moscow.

Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled and one destroyed the drone after authorities decided it posed a potential threat to the hundreds of people working at the site and to critical energy infrastructure.

Defence Minister Radu Miruță said the drone was carrying explosives and that Kyiv had confirmed it was not Ukrainian.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the incident as part of "an escalating campaign of threats" against the European Union.

"This is hybrid warfare," she said, accusing those responsible of seeking to unsettle European citizens and divide the bloc.

High alert

Europe as a whole is on high alert after drone flyovers into NATO airspace reached an unprecedented scale last September, prompting European leaders to agree to develop a "drone wall" along their borders to better detect, track and intercept drones violating Europe's airspace.

In November, NATO military officials said a new US anti-drone system had been deployed to the alliance’s eastern flank.

And following a violation of Polish airspace, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced the formation of the Eastern Sentry programme, which aims to deter further Russian incursions.

A French military AWACS surveillance plane operates cockpit equipment on a 10-hour mission to Romania, 9 January, 2024 AP Photo

Some European officials described the incidents as Moscow testing NATO’s response, which raised questions about how prepared the alliance is against potential threats from Russia.

The Kremlin has dismissed allegations that Russia is behind some of the unidentified drone flights in Europe as "unfounded."

World.title: Panama Canal to reduce shipping as El Niño fuels drought in lakes that feed waterway
World.content:
The Panama Canal will cut the number of ships passing through it starting next month because of drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, the operator of the strategic waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific said.

 

From 3 September, the number of vessels allowed through each day will fall from 36 to 34 due to lower water levels in two artificial lakes that feed the canal, the Panama Canal Authority said.

It will drop to 32 from 15 September onward, the agency said.

Central America is in the throes of a severe drought driven by El Niño, a weather pattern that warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall.

In the area of the canal rainfall from May to August is down by 34% from its historical average, the authority said, adding that El Niño could cut it even more.

The Panama Canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and around 40% of US container traffic.

The canal operator said that "lower than forecast rainfall in the canal's watershed" called for measures to bolster the "long-term sustainability" of the waterway.

It has already implemented other water conservation measures, such as lowering the maximum draft, the vessel's depth in the water, for the largest ships.

In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low the waterway's operators cut the daily ship transit number from 38 to 22.

It said that with the upcoming reduction, waiting times for ships trying to get through without making a reservation beforehand will increase.

Nine of 10 ships using the canal do so with a reservation and the remaining slots are auctioned off.

Before the Iran war the average winning bid in these auctions was $135,000 (€115,000). But in April one shipping company eager to use the canal paid a whopping $4 million (€3.4 million).

A cargo ship traverses the Cocoli Locks of the Panama Canal, 9 August, 2026 AP Photo

The operator said it does not rule out further restrictions on shipping depending on how much it rains in the coming weeks.

The US-built canal's main users are the United States, China, Japan, Chile and South Korea.

Water is a touchy issue in Panama because the lakes that feed the canal also provide water for half the population of 4.2 million people.

El Niño occurs on average every two to seven years and this year's is shaping up as one of the strongest on record.

World.title: Dog tags and bones: How experts are identifying WWII soldiers found in the Danube
World.content:
The unusually low water level of the Danube in Budapest has revealed relics that had remained hidden on the riverbed for more than 80 years. Among the discoveries are the remains of two German soldiers from the Second World War, their military identity tags and a DKW military motorcycle buried in the mud.

 

For decades, the fate of the two soldiers was unknown. They were listed as missing, with no confirmation of where or how they had died. Now, the discovery of their remains and identity tags could finally help establish who they were.

The identity tags could help clarify the identity of the soldiers whose remains have been found. Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge e.V.

Military identity tags were designed to identify fallen soldiers. Each carried a unique number and could be broken into two parts after a soldier's death. One half remained with the body, while the other was sent to the relevant authorities so that the death could be recorded and relatives informed.

"If he had been killed, his comrades would have broken the identity tag," explains Norbert Hambuch, cemetery manager at the Budaörs German war cemetery. "The upper part with the two holes stays with the soldier, and his comrades take the lower part and send it to the central office."

Hambuch was translating for Euronews his colleague Gabor Kohlrusz, who works as a reburial specialist for the German War Graves Commission, the Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge.

But finding an identity tag alongside human remains does not automatically establish the person's identity. Where exactly the tag is discovered can provide an important clue.

"If an identity tag is discovered at chest level, it probably belongs to the dead soldier because he would have worn it around his neck," Diane Tempel-Bornett of the Volksbund told Euronews. "At hip level, an identity tag is more likely to indicate that it was in a trouser pocket and that the dead soldier had taken it from another dead comrade in order to return it to their unit."

After the Second World War, large numbers of soldiers were listed as missing, leaving their families uncertain about whether they had been killed or survived. The two men whose remains lay undiscovered in the Danube were among them.

The Volksbund is now working with its Hungarian partner to establish their identities. The remains are expected to be buried at the Budaörs war cemetery outside Budapest later this year.

One of the identity tags recovered from the Danube belonged to a Wehrmacht soldier, while the other was issued to a member of the Waffen-SS. Investigators must still establish whether the tags actually belonged to the two men whose remains were recovered. Any preliminary identification by the Volksbund must then be officially confirmed by Germany's Federal Archives.

Second World War wreckage emerges from the Danube

The discovery comes as other remnants of the Second World War have emerged from the unusually low waters of the Danube.

One find in particular has attracted attention: a DKW military motorcycle that had been buried in the mud for more than 80 years. Together with Gabor Kohlrusz and Norbert Hambuch, Euronews returned to the site where it was recovered.

"There were a great many wrecks here, vehicles from the final phase of the war in Budapest. All this debris was pushed down here directly after the war, and only later were these rocks piled on top," Hambuch explains.

The Battle of Budapest lasted 102 days in 1944 and 1945, with tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians killed. The motorcycle recovered from the river is eventually expected to form part of an exhibition commemorating the fighting.

"We have an extensive collection of equipment from the Second World War," says Imre Kovacs, the Volksbund's representative in Hungary.

He describes the recovered DKW motorcycle as a "showpiece" for an exhibition at the Institute and Museum of Military History, the Volksbund's Hungarian partner. The motorcycle has since been cleaned and is expected to go on display there.

Soviet and Romanian troops fought in Budapest in 1945 against German and Hungarian units. AP Photo

The soldiers' remains have meanwhile been taken to the Volksbund's facilities at Budaörs.

"The bones have been collected and taken to the depot, that is, to the Volksbund's largest military cemetery in Hungary, Budaörs," Hambuch says. "There they are cleaned, recorded anthropologically, documented and, in the autumn, in October, they will be buried together with the other soldiers found this year."

But the work of locating and identifying those missing from the Second World War is far from over.

"On the territory of the former USSR alone, around two million soldiers from the Second World War are still missing," Tempel-Bornett says. "For Hungary, losses are put at around 54,000. Since 1992 we have exhumed and reburied 29,956 dead in Hungary."

More than eight decades after their deaths, the two men recovered from the Danube may now finally receive a grave, potentially bearing their names.

For the Volksbund and Hungary's Institute and Museum of Military History, identifying and reburying the dead is also part of their wider work of remembrance and reconciliation.

World.title: Ghent University suspends US academic behind Jason Arday plagiarism charges
World.content:
A Belgian university suspended a US academic on Thursday who spearheaded accusations of plagiarism against Jason Arday, the black ex-Cambridge professor found dead last week after resigning over the scandal.

 

Researcher Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined "race realist" who was himself sacked from his Cambridge post two years ago, posted on X: "I was just suspended by Ghent University. They will almost certainly fire me."

Without naming Cofnas, the University of Ghent said in a statement it had launched a "preliminary disciplinary investigation" against a postdoctoral researcher embroiled in the furore, suspending him "as a precautionary measure."

Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest-ever black professor when he was appointed in 2023, was found dead Friday aged 41.

He was facing mounting accusations he had plagiarised parts of his doctoral thesis and exaggerated some of his personal life achievements.

Diagnosed with autism and other developmental difficulties as a child, Arday had disputed the allegations against him.

But he quit on 5 August, writing in his resignation letter that he had "reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure."

Plagiarism concerns surrounding Arday first surfaced several years ago but went nowhere at the time, with one reporter backing down from investigating further after the professor threatened legal action.

Last month, however, Cofnas came forward to say he had found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work and the case snowballed, receiving widespread media coverage in Britain and the United States.

British media and right-wing commentators seized on the row, claiming Arday had unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.

Ghent University said it was now "assessing" whether there were sufficient grounds to launch full disciplinary proceedings in the case.

Former Cambridge University professor Jason Arday @PolitlcsUK

In a previous statement on Wednesday, the university said it was "shocked" by Arday's death and took "very seriously" public statements made by its researcher regarding the former professor.

"Ghent University stands for respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism," said the statement by the university's rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert.

"We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial," it added.

"However, that freedom is not unlimited. It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others."

World.title: Diamonds or duds: Are these the most overrated albums of all time?
World.content:
There are certain albums which no one dares to disgrace or reappraise.

 

You know the ones: records that are revered by practically everyone and which every self-respecting music fan is expected to cherish. But are these albums truly untouchable, or are we blindly regurgitating accepted wisdom?

The Euronews Culture team bares all and takes a hard listen at 12 so-called ‘masterpieces’ and asks: ‘Isn’t it about time we admitted that these aren’t the sacrosanct triumphs they’re made out to be?’

Different strokes for different folks, of course - we wouldn't want to break any levees. Speaking of which, we start with...

Led Zeppelin – IV (1971)

IV Atlantic

It’s the album that gave us 'Stairway to Heaven', perhaps the greatest rock song ever made. It’s widely considered Led Zeppelin’s pinnacle of achievement. It’s essential listening, a rock'n'roll classic. And yet… Look, Led Zeppelin’s fourth album opens like a firehose on a scorching summer day. 'Black Dog' and 'Rock and Roll' knock you off your feet. It’s incredible. Later, you get the transcendent 'Stairway to Heaven' and smooth 'Going to California'. But is it as complete an experience as we’re supposed to believe it is? I’m not so sure.The highs do the heavy lifting, and it’s fair to wonder if they distort our view of the work in its entirety – if the band’s greater mythology hasn’t generated some revisionism. The problem is that once an album is declared the masterpiece, everything else gets measured against it. But Zeppelin made more adventurous records. 'Led Zeppelin III' is restless and eclectic, and 'Physical Graffiti' takes bigger swings across a kaleidoscopic double LP. For all its brilliance, 'IV' shouldn’t have a monopoly on Led Zeppelin’s legacy. CS

Eagles – Hotel California (1976)

Hotel California Asylum

Remember that scene in The Big Lebowski when The Dude gets into an altercation with a cab driver when he asks him to change the radio station? "I've had a rough night, and I hate the fucking Eagles, man!" says our favourite stoner. Well, I loudly cheer for The Dude every single time. The Eagles are rubbish, and their most famous album proves it. Not that many would agree, as 'Hotel California' is the sixth-most sold record of all time, with reported global sales of around 44 million copies. To add insult to injury, their greatest hits album remains the best-selling album of all time in the US. Makes you think, don't it? The band's so-called 1976 "rock classic" is chockablock with thoroughly mediocre songs about being good looking in the desert, good looking driving around LA, good looking on the street, and good looking while asking questions like "Should I stay or go? I really want to know / Would I lose or win if I try and love again?" I don't know about the latter part of your inquiry, that's your business and good luck to you. As for the second part, go. Please go away. DM

Fleetwood Mac – Rumours (1977)

Rumours Warner Bros.

I was on a five-hour road trip with two of my best mates, and we decided to spend it doing something that felt vaguely productive: listening, front to back, to albums considered some of the greatest ever made. We started with MJ’s 'Thriller' - brilliant, pretty much faultless, bar perhaps that eye-rollingly saccharine McCartney duet. Then 'The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill': beautiful, soulful, genuinely sublime. So when we arrived at Fleetwood Mac’s 'Rumours' we were expecting our lives to be changed. They sadly weren’t. That isn’t to say 'Rumours' is bad. It’s often excellent. 'Dreams' is arguably one of the greatest songs ever recorded; 'Go Your Own Way' remains an absolute bop; and the iconic bassline and euphoric release of 'The Chain' is top notch. But taken as a whole, the album left all three of us strangely unmoved. Remove all the relationship drama and mythology attached to it and what remains is often remarkably safe, polished, and occasionally beige. 'Second Hand News' is a strangely forgettable opener; 'Don’t Stop' is irritatingly chirpy; and 'Oh Daddy' is frankly a bit of a snooze. In the days after I listened to 'Tusk' and 'Tango in the Night', two of the band's later albums, and both struck me as more adventurous and interesting. _'_Rumours'has a handful of perfect songs, but it’s by no means a perfect album. TF

Pink Floyd - The Wall (1979)

The Wall Harvest/EMI

God help me, I love a concept album and Pink Floyd rarely disappointed in this regard. However, their 1979 rock opera – while a towering achievement narratively speaking – is a listening experience that never resonated with me. Put bluntly: it bored me to death whilst depressing me at the same time. Granted, the double-album is meant to be punishing, mirroring the themes of abandonment and isolation wished for by chief architect and gloom meister general Roger Waters. However, 'The Wall' always felt bloated, replete with heavy-handed metaphors and more filler than any other album they'd released until then. 'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2', 'Hey You' and 'Comfortably Numb' are gems, there's no doubt about that - but that's three standouts in a comfortably plump 26-song slog of a tracklist. And when you look back at the band's discography, every concept album that preceded 'The Wall' continues to surpass it. Give me 'The Dark Side of the Moon' (the original, not that trash version Waters put out three years ago), 'Wish You Were Here' and 'Animals' any day of the week over this one. DM

AC/DC - Back In Black (1980)

Back in Black Albert/Atlantic

Here's the thing with AC/DC... Every tedious riff in their repetive song collection sticks to the same ear-bleedingly naff blue-collar rock formula - so much so that each "hit" sounds completely indistinguishable from the one that preceded it. You could play me tracks from 'Back In Black', 'Highway To Hell' or any of their other 16 albums (yes, I counted), and I'd stare at you blankly like a deflated basset hound yearning for the sweet release of variety. Or tinnitus. Either will do. The defense rests. Your witness. DM

Prince – Purple Rain (1984)

Purple Rain Warner Bros.

An Oscar. Two Grammys. A No. 1 album that spent 24 weeks atop the Billboard 200. More than 25 million copies sold worldwide. 'Purple Rain' has been canonised as one of the defining albums of the 1980s. And I understand why. Prince was an absurdly talented musician - guitarist, pianist, producer, songwriter, vocalist - and the sheer amount of creativity and craft on display is difficult to deny. But perhaps that’s the problem: 'Purple Rain' sometimes feels like Prince desperately trying to prove he can do everything at once. Guitar solos, key changes, falsetto runs - every song seems determined to throw the entire Prince toolbox at you. The result can be exhilarating like the ending of 'The Beautiful Ones', but it can also feel wildly overcooked, overly-theatrical and exhausting. And lyrically, the album can be surprisingly… thin. For all the hype surrounding Prince as a genius songwriter, some of his stuff like on 'Take Me With U’ is pretty disposable. And as for the title track, yes, it's a classic, no argument there. But does it really need to run for 8 minutes and 41 seconds? I've got places to be, Prince. Things to do! TF

The Smiths – The Queen Is Dead (1986)

The Queen Is Dead Rough Trade

I’ll preface this by saying that, unlike Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of Summer, I personally do not “love The Smiths.” In fact, I think the “For Britain” badge-wearing Morrissey is a whiny, pitchless, pompous moron, so don't expect neutrality here. 'The Queen Is Dead' is one of those albums that seems contractually obliged to appear on every “Greatest Albums of All Time” list, and is regularly hailed as The Smiths’ masterpiece. And I get some of the hype. Johnny Marr’s guitar work is immaculate, the band sounds sharp throughout, the opening track is electric and 'There Is a Light That Never Goes Out' is, dare I say, charmingly catchy. But there are also some absolute stinkers on this thing. 'Frankly, Mr. Shankly' is a twee, irritating novelty song that I cannot understand anyone willingly putting on twice, while 'Vicar in a Tutu' is an even more baffling detour. Even 'Some Girls Are Bigger Than Others' feels like an oddly limp way to close what is supposedly a classic. Maybe I'm missing something. Or maybe Morrissey's voice and ego have just worn me down. Either way - masterpiece? Not convinced. TF

Oasis – Definitely Maybe (1994)

Definitely Maybe Creation

While I wouldn't brazenly affirm that Oasis as a whole is overrated, I will die on the following hill: their debut album is held to unreasonably high regard. Yes, 'Definitely Maybe' was the soundtrack to a new grunge-ending / Britpop striggering era, but the hype around it ever since its release has been exhausting. The singles are catchy, and no one is denying Noel Gallagher's knack for a singalong chorus; but the rest is filler, with lyrics which are either uninspired or the work of someone operating on a full nappy. As for Liam's efforts, there's a reason why his delivery of lines "Toniiiiiiiight I'm a rock 'n' roll staaaar" and "Sun-sheeeee-iiiiiii-ne" have been memed to death. Far from biblical, r'kid. Ultimately, Oasis is a terrific singles band; but when it comes to cohesive albums, the only LP which truly works as a consistent whole was - somewhat ironically - their B-side compilation 'The Masterplan', which remains their best release. As much as I'm aware of my own hang-ups when it comes to the parodical swagger of certain 'Madferit' Oasis fans, you can deify them all you want but two things remain true: 1) As good as they can be, they weren't the saviours of British rock'n'roll; and 2) Their contemporaries Blur, Pulp and Super Furry Animals were significantly more innovative. Fight me. DM

Kanye West – Graduation (2007)

Graduation Roc-A-Fella/Def Jam

It’s easy to dunk on Ye these days. The man has said some heinous things – so heinous that he was banned from performing in most of Europe. Now, of course, he’s set to take the stage in Russia, which only reinforces his painful spiral into pariah status. Separate the art from the artist, though, and we can appreciate that West’s run of albums is almost unrivalled in contemporary hip-hop. His first six albums were groundbreaking in their own ways. But 'Graduation' isn’t the pop-rap masterpiece it’s hailed to be. Released in 2007, it was engineered for arenas, with huge hooks, gleaming synths and U2-level production. Yes, it helped move mainstream hip-hop toward a more melodic and experimental realm, but 'Graduation' seems shallow and meaningless in comparison to the grander statements Ye made with 'My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy' or 'Yeezus'. It’s more a triumph of commercial instinct than artistic revelation. For an artist who has always been at his best when he’s being unpredictable – even, perhaps unfortunately, now – 'Graduation' is surprisingly conventional. CS

Arcade Fire – The Suburbs (2010)

The Suburbs Merge/City Slang/Mercury

A decade before frontman Win Butler was outed as a manipulative creep, Arcade Fire reached previously unreached heights for an indie band. In 2011, The Suburbs scored a surprise Grammy win for Album of the Year. Arcade Fire had made it. The album is a 64-minute paean to lost youth and white-bread suburban ennui, full of smooth hooks, mid-tempo guitars and open-road anthems. It’s not a bad listen, if you’re able to divorce Butler’s allegations of sexual misconduct from the experience. In fact, it’s largely enjoyable. But Album of the Year was a stretch then and more of one now. Lyrics like “Rococo, rococo, rococo / Oh, they’re breaking my heart” and “I feel like I’ve been living in / A city with no children in it” are comically overwritten (or underwritten, depending on your perspective). And compared with today’s ambient despair, the schlocky air of suburban angst and coming-of-age theme seem ridiculous in retrospect. CS

Daft Punk - Random Access Memories (2013)

Random Access Memories Columbia

Hailed as a triumphant comeback album after the disappointing 'Human After All' (2005), Daft Punk's fourth and final LP paid tribute to 70s and 80s music – specifically disco and funk. The line-up of collaborators was impressive, with the French electro pioneers recruiting Giorgio Moroder, Pharrell Williams, Nile Rodgers and Julian Casablancas for what was to be their swansong. While it came out to universal acclaim, I'd argue that even if the sonic nostalgia blast was welcome in the moment and their ubiquitous single 'Get Lucky' was inescapably good, 'Random Access Memories' still gets far too much praise. When listening to the Grammy winning LP from start to finish, its pacing isn't as great as you remember, a lot of tracks feel indulgent, and it's... well, clumsy. I suspect the marketing team in charge of the album's rollout is partly responsible for its lingering acclaim, as fans will remember a teaser campaign which worked wonders. But when push comes to shove, 'RAM' may not be le plus faible in the robotic duo's discography, but it is far from their chef-d'oeuvre. Don't get me started on that dire drumless 2023 re-release, which was a complete waste of time. DM

Taylor Swift – Folklore (2020)

Folklore Republic

When Taylor Swift released 'folklore', I was editing a plucky city magazine in Bangkok and not having a great time of it. About five songs into the swirling 16-track album, I remember telling myself: “This is why the editing profession exists.” Look, Swift doesn’t need my praise for her prowess as a songwriter. She has 14 Grammys and about a billion US dollars to prove her merits. Her canon is largely great. But 'folklore' was the first sign that the ego was perhaps outgrowing the artist. The pivot to piano-driven sweater-weather music was a welcome change and hardly a surprise, considering Swift worked with The National’s Aaron Dessner. But was Dessner the editor she needed? Could anyone edit her? When the album is good ('this is me trying'), it’s very good. When it’s not ('betty', 'illicit affairs'), you wish someone had stepped in to propose some surgical cuts. Looking back on it, 'folklore' marked a turning point for Swift. Since then, her once sharp lyricism has become head-scratching (see: 'Fortnight' and 'epiphany'), and her albums have become increasingly self-indulgent and bloated. CS

There we have it. Heroic takedowns or utter blasphemy? Feel free to get in touch. Just don't bother if you're defending the Eagles. Life's too short.

World.title: Panama Canal to cap ship transits due to El Nino drought
World.content:
Panama Canal will cut daily transits of ships from September because of low rainfall and amid an intensifying El Nimo event.

The Panama Canal will cut the number of ships passing through it starting next month due to a lack of rainfall as the El Nino weather pattern takes hold over the region, the canal operator said on Thursday.

The vital waterway that links two oceans and carries about 5% of global maritime trade relies on rainfall to keep ships moving through the passageway.

From September 3, the waterway will allow 34 ships to pass through it, instead of the current 36, the Panama Canal Authority said.

From September 15, the number of ships allowed to pass through it will drop to 32.

That Panama is met with severe drought even though it is one of the wettest nations on Earth is a sign that El Nino has formed in a warmed-up Pacific Ocean. Rainfall between May and August was about 34% below the historical average for the period, the canal operator said.

What is El Nino?

El Nino is characterized by unusually warm ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific, with knock-on effects including droughts, floods and wildfires.

Those changes in winds and ocean temperatures have knock-on effects on weather patterns all over the world and will likely turbocharge extreme weather events because of how warm the world already is from fossil fuel pollution, experts say.

Scientists say they expect El Nino to get so intense this late fall and early winter that "it would rank among the largest El Nino events in the historical record going back to 1950."

How climate change is teaming up with 'Super El Nino' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Panama Canal affected by drought in recent years

The 50-mile (80-kilometer) Panama Canal was impacted by severe drought in 2023-2024, when the canal operator slashed ship crossings.

In 2023, the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low the waterway's operators cut the daily ship transit number from 38 to 22.

The authority has already implemented water conservation measures but called for methods to bolster the "long-term sustainability" of the waterway.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Alaska charter flight crash kills 8
World.content:
A small ‌Cessna 441 plane operated by a private charter company crashed near a US military-managed radar site in Alaska. All on board have reportedly died.

A charter plane crash at a remote military radar site in western Alaska on Thursday has left all eight people on board dead, according to the United States military.

The aircraft crashed around 12:15 pm (2015 UTC) on approach to Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, located about 725 kilometers (450 miles) west of Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, from where it had departed.

Six passengers and two pilots were aboard the plane during the incident, said Clint Johnson, Alaska region chief of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

Reports identified the plane as a ‌Cessna 441 operated by Anchorage-based air charter company Security Aviation.

Alaska Senator Lisa Murkowski expressed her condolences, following news of the crash.

"I've traveled extensively with Security Aviation throughout Alaska, and have met many of their experienced pilots," she said on X, naming the charter company that operates in the remote region.

She added that multiple agencies, including the US Coast Guard, NTSB, Alaska State Troopers, and the Rescue Coordination Center had responded to the crash.

Air Force Alaskan Command mourns 'loss for our military family'

The Associated Press cited the US ​military's Alaskan Command as saying that the plane was a "civilian-contracted aircraft."

The passengers on board were "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment," AP quoted Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, as saying in a statement.

The specifics of what work the crash victims were doing at the radar site — which tracks aircraft operating in Alaskan airspace — was not immediately clear from the Alaskan Command's statement.

"This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said, according to AP.

The Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center manages the radar site.

World.title: India news: MP's son booked, not arrested after fatal crash in Hyderabad
World.content:
Skip next section MP's son booked after fatal Hyderabad crash, but not arrested

08/21/2026 August 21, 2026 MP's son booked after fatal Hyderabad crash, but not arrested

The 21-year-old son of a parliamentarian has been booked for allegedly driving an Aston Martin that struck and killed a 26-year-old woman in Hyderabad, media reports said.

Lingamaneni Sanjush allegedly hit a pedestrian while she was crossing the road in the Madhapur area of ​​the city on Sunday. She suffered severe head injuries and was taken to a hospital, where she was declared dead.

Sanjush is the son of Rajya Sabha member Lingamaneni Ramesh of the Jana Sena Party, which is part of the ruling alliance with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in Andhra Pradesh.

Police booked Sanjush for rash and negligent driving, an offense that carries a maximum sentence of five years. He has not been arrested because the police said the offense is bailable, and authorities have issued him a notice, reports said.

The case is reminiscent of the 2024 Pune Porsche case, in which a 17-year-old driver allegedly under the influence of alcohol killed two people.

The teenager was granted bail by the Juvenile Justice Board within hours of the crash and ordered, under other conditions, to write a 300-word essay on road accidents.

The decision triggered widespread public outrage over what was seen as lenient treatment.

The Pune case also led to allegations of attempts to cover up the accident, including claims of efforts to influence the investigation and manipulate evidence.

World.title: Morocco: Migrants caught between Ceuta dreams and reality
World.content:
The Moroccan city of Fnideq is next to Spanish-controlled Ceuta. In Fnideq, would-be migrants dream of crossing to a better life, even as locals who witnessed recent mass migration surges say it's way too risky.

There are only a few kilometers between the city of Fnideq in Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta — but the distance between those who dream of crossing that divide and those who chose to stay in Morocco is far greater than that.

After July 30, when an estimated 72,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, there were further calls on social media for people to come to Fnideq for another mass crossing attempt in mid-August.

That is despite the fact that around 100 people died in the July attempt and that most of those who crossed into Ceuta have since returned to Morocco. Numbers are unclear but somewhere between 2,000 and 8,000 of those who managed to get over to the Spanish enclave remain there. According to reports, they are now living in desperate circumstances. Many are sleeping on the beach while they wait for Spanish authorities to decide their fate.

Homeless and desperate in Morocco

Still, back in Morocco, some would-be migrants continue to hope for a chance to get to Ceuta.

Malika came to Fnideq from the city of Casablanca in western Morocco with her two children after she heard that people had managed to get there on July 30; she did not want to give DW her full name for personal reasons.

"My life is below zero," she said, with tears in her eyes. "I have no life."

Most of the people who crossed into Ceuta have returned to Morocco Image: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP

Malika heard there might be a new opportunity to cross in August so she has stayed in Fnideq, together with her 3-year-old daughter and 8-year-old son. For the past few weeks, she says she has simply wandered the streets searching for ways to feed her children. The family has slept in the open.

But rumors about an August crossing also reached both Spanish and Moroccan authorities. On August 15, eyewitnesses reported a heavy Moroccan security presence around Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish exclave to the east, with numerous checkpoints, patrol boats monitoring the coast and water cannons stationed at the border. Moroccan police said they arrested 111 people as they tried to enter Ceuta.

There was no mass crossing on August 15 and Malika has remained in Fnideq.

"I'm in a situation where I might do something to myself at any moment," she told DW. "My children are starving. I'm practically homeless. I have no job and no stable home, and my husband suffers from depression due to extreme poverty. Sometimes he just disappears, leaving me alone with the two children, without money or shelter."

That is why she still wants to get to Ceuta, she says, where she is certain she and the children will find support of some kind: "Our situation is very difficult. … that's why I want them to go to Ceuta. They will study there and we will be fine."

Why young Moroccans risked everything to reach Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

No future, no hope

Another man that DW meets in Fnideq, Ahmed Amhid, is in a better position. He's 22 years old and he came from Oued Zem in central Morocco after hearing about the August crossing. He is with a relative selling drinks on the street.

Amhid says there are no job opportunities in his hometown and he feels like there's no future for him there.

"The situation is deplorable, there's nothing in this country," he says angrily. "I want to emigrate from Morocco. I have no hope in this country."

Amhid pauses to offer a glass of orange juice to a customer before continuing.

"There's nothing in this country: no jobs, no industries, no companies, nothing," he told DW. "My current income isn't enough to support me or build a future."

Many of the young people, like Amhid, who arrived in Fnideq recently came because of what they had seen on social media, explains Ahmed al-Dafri, a Moroccan expert on media and culture.

'No future at home': Ahmed Amhid came from central Morocco to Fnideq hoping to cross into Ceuta Image: Zhor Baki/DW

This kind of online call represents "a new model of digital mobilization that doesn't necessarily require a single leader or a central authority," al-Dafri told DW. "When videos circulate widely, especially those documenting past successful attempts to cross, it creates a feeling that everyone wants to migrate and that no one wants to stay."

This type of content can give people a feeling of exclusion if they don't join in the collective movement, he explains.

Not everybody wants to leave Morocco

Nearer to the border between the city and Ceuta, DW meets Mohamed al-Dami. The 30-year-old says he isn't even thinking about leaving Morocco, even though he watched many people try recently.

The economic situation is unstable in this country, he concedes.

"But personally, I've never thought about migrating. I buy, sell and work normally," he explains. "I could migrate, but I won't throw myself into the sea in an attempt that might not even end with me reaching my destination. Even if you get into Ceuta, it's not worth all the trouble and risk. Why put yourself in harm's way?"

Local trader Mohamed al-Dami watched crowds trying to leave Fnideq but he doesn't think the risk is worth it Image: Zhor Baki / DW

Al-Dami recalled seeing crowds heading for the border in late July. He was never tempted to join them.

"In my opinion, if a person can make a living and secure their future, then praise be to God. As for the future, it is in God's hands," he says.

He also heard the calls to try and cross into Ceuta again on August 15, but given all the security preparations, he didn't think those trying to cross would be successful anyway.

"Honestly, since a large number of young people entered Ceuta and then returned here again, people's morale has really plummeted and there's not much enthusiasm for this sort of thing at all," al-Dami said.

Migrants bring change to city

Another local man, Munir Hamdouch, a 34-year-old merchant, tells DW that he too has never thought about emigrating.

Things are not easy here, he admits. He's been working in his field since 2012 and he's noticed a huge decrease in tourism in Fnideq, which impacts those working in seasonal trade.

"We want an economic revival in this city," he adds. "Projects are either stalled, or maybe they've been built but haven't been opened yet. The city really needs economic alternatives."

Local civil society activist Mohamed Azzouz agreed that things have changed in Fnideq because of migration. The city was no longer a transit point for migrants, instead it had become a base for them, he says.

Migration has economic, social and cultural impacts in the city and it has become "an integral part" of Fnideq's identity. That in turn has impacted the city's appeal for tourists as well as its economy, Azzouz says.

Another Fnideq man, Munir Hamdouch, says he wouldn't leave Morocco because his work and family is here Image: Zhor Baki/DW

Despite all that, local trader Hamdouch is not thinking about leaving.

"I have my shop and my family with young children so even if the thought crossed my mind, I wouldn't be able to," he explained. "For me, if I just earn 100 dirhams and I can feed my children, then I thank God."

Hamdouch thinks that some of the people who try to cross into Ceuta are chasing an impossible dream.

"Some people lack patience and are never satisfied," he suggests. "It's also a matter of contentment. Some people just want something better, they want everything."

World.title: Guatemala says it received nearly 2,300 US-deported Mexicans
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's administration is ramping up third country deportations, with Mexican deportees being sent to Guatemala and reportedly Honduras in the past year.

The United States has deported and sent some 2,300 Mexicans to Guatemala this year in a shifting Trump administration practice that Mexico opposes.

Mexican deportees from the US, until recently, were largely sent directly back to their country, with only a few arriving in other countries.

On Wednesday, Guatemalan President Bernardo Arevalo confirmed that 2,284 Mexicans deported from the US have arrived in his Central American country so far this year.

"They are arriving in planes of Guatemalan ‌returnees," Arevalo ⁠said ⁠in a televised interview.

He said the deported Mexicans are arriving in a "transit stopover" before being taken to Mexico as part of an "arrangement" with Mexico's government.

Arevalo said the Mexican deportees were transferred to their home country within 24 hours, with Mexico or the US covering the transportation costs.

What has Mexico said about the US deportations?

On Thursday, Mexico's Foreign Ministry voiced its objection to the US practice and said that it was coordinating with the countries involved to ensure the safe repatriation of its nationals.

"The Mexican government has expressed its opposition to this practice to US authorities and has reiterated that every Mexican citizen has the right to enter the country," it asserted.

The ministry did not give any details on the number of cases or costs.

What is the US' third country deportation policy under Trump?

As per international accords, migrants may be sent to third countries if their home country rejects them or if it is unsafe for them to be sent back. Otherwise, they should be directly deported back to their country of citizenship.

The Trump administration has however been using third-country deportations to send back migrants, striking bilateral agreements with several countries, including Mexico, to receive migrants from other countries.

Immigration experts say that by sending Mexicans through Guatemala or other third countries, thereby moving them farther from the US-Mexico border, the US wants to make it more difficult for them to cross back into its territory.

Mexicans sent back via Honduras: reports

According to reports, some Mexicans deported by the US were also being sent to Honduras.

The Associated Press cited official documents from Honduras as showing that 82 Mexican deportees from the US arrived in the city of San Pedro Sula aboard two flights last week, with an additional 35 who were due to arrive Thursday.

There was no immediate statement from the Honduran government.

According to the'Third Country Deportation Watch' tracker of Human Rights First and Refugees International, Honduras received 165 Mexicans by mid-July and another 37 Mexicans have been deported from the US to Honduras by mid-August so far.

In a press release this week , the organizations deemed the third country transfers by the US government as an "opaque and cruel system," saying that "thousands of individuals have been subjected to arbitrary detention, family separations, and chain refoulement in third countries."

World.title: Hong Kong convicts activists in national security trial
World.content:
The two pro-democracy Tiananmen activists were found guilty of inciting subversion. The high profile case has been widely criticized for highlighting the deterioration of freedom of expression.

A Hong Kong court on Thursday convicted two pro-democracy Tiananmen activists tried under Beijing's controversial national security law for "incitement to subversion."

Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, had organized candlelight vigils to mark Beijing's deadly 1989 Tiananmen crackdown. They were charged in 2021 and both pleaded not guilty.

They face a maximum prison term of 10 years and are expected to be sentenced at a later date.

What else do we know about the charges against the pro-democracy activists?

The pair "incited other persons to organize, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power", a press summary handed out to reporters said.

Prosecutors had argued they "endanger(ed) national security in the name of human rights."

Public commemoration of the deadly Tiananmen crackdown, when Beijing sent troops and tanks to crush protests calling for political reform in and around the capital's Tiananmen Square, have been effectively banned since the 2020 imposition of the national security law on Hong Kong.

The controversial law came after Hong Kong's 2019 massive anti-government, pro-democracy protests.

World.title: Pakistan: Former PM Khan briefly moved to private hospital
World.content:
Khan was examined by a team of doctors before being moved back to prison. The former PM's supporters say his health has deteriorated during more than ​three years behind bars since being removed from office in 2022.

Pakistan's former Prime ‌Minister ⁠Imran ⁠Khan was briefly transferred ​from ​jail ‌to a private hospital on Friday.

"Former Prime Minister Imran Khan ‌has ​been shifted from Adiala Jail to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad following Supreme Court order," a spokesperson from his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party (PTI) said in a text message to journalists.

Later on Friday, the PTI and Pakistani authorities said Khan had been moved back to prison.

"A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist, and a physician, conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit," Information Minister Attaullah Tarar wrote on X.

Dozens of Khan supporters had gathered near the hospital, the French AFP news agency reported, while security was deployed in anticipation of the former prime minister's arrival.

What else do we know about Khan's hospital transfer?

The move comes after the Supreme Court this week ordered Khan's transfer to the private hospital within 48 hours.

It was initially seen as a potential first step toward easing tensions between Khan's party and Pakistan's powerful military establishment, which have been at odds since ‌his removal from office in 2022.

Khan's transfer comes amid some government opposition to the Supreme Court order, including from Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar who had argued that a convicted prisoner must be treated inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law.

Tarar added that he was requesting Khan's medical tests be carried out at a government hospital instead of a private facility.

Security was deployed to the Shifa International Hospital in anticipation of Khan's transfer Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

But later, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said the government would fully comply with the Supreme Court’s ruling and that its request for clarification was not intended to defy or delay implementation of the decision.

Khan's supporters say his health has deteriorated during more than ​three years in prison.

His lawyers said he has lost significant vision in his right eye, but the government had previously said medical reports disclosed no condition requiring immediate ⁠treatment.

Khan's fall from prime minister to prisoner

Khan was Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. The cricketer-turned-politician has been in prison since 2023, following his ouster in a no-confidence vote.

He was convicted on a number of charges including allegations of an unlawful marriage and corruption. He was sentenced late last year, along with his wife, to 17 years in prison for graft. Both deny wrongdoing and Khan has maintained that his charges are politically motivated.

PTI still enjoys significant support across key provinces in Pakistan, and Khan himself remains a popular figure. His arrest in early 2023 triggered nationwide protests that resulted in hundreds of people being arrested.

His PTI party told Reuters they were planning a nationwide march on September 27 to demand access to Khan, speedy hearings in his case and his release.

World.title: Peru: Strong earthquake shakes southern Andes
World.content:
The quake has a magnitude of 6.7 according to the US Geological Survey, while Peru's Geophysical Institute put the figure even higher. There are no immediate reports of casualties.

A powerful earthquake shook Peru's southern Andes Mountains on Thursday, measured at magnitude 6.7 by the US Geological Survey (USGS) and 7.2 by Peru's Geophysical Institute (IGP).

The USGS said the quake occurred at 1 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) with an epicenter 38 kilometers (24 miles) northwest of the town of Upahuacho, in the southern Ayacucho region, and a depth of 66.7 kilometers. The IGP had the depth at 108 kilometers.

The earthquake "was felt with moderate to strong intensity in several departments," the National Institute of Civil Defense wrote on social media.

Images broadcast by Peruvian media showed rocks and earth tumbling down hills around Coracora, the closest significant town to the epicenter with a population of about 10,000.

What damage has the Peru earthquake caused?

There were no immediate reports of damage or casualties and the Peruvian Navy confirmed there was no threat of a tsunami.

"The population has responded, they evacuated and took shelter," Coracora mayor Yony Odon told local television.

Luis Vasquez, head of Civil Defense, told local radio station RPP that "no damage of any kind has been reported so far."

The jolt was felt across several regions of southern Peru, including Ica and Arequipa. Reporters for the AFP news agency said tremors were even felt as far away as the capital, Lima.

A 5.1 magnitude earthquake in the Andes region of Peru late on July 18, 2026, killed five people and injured 21 [FILE: July 18, 2026] Image: Peruvian Ministry of Defense/AFP

How common are earthquakes in Peru?

Earthquakes are frequent in Peru which lies on the southeastern edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire," an area of frequent seismic activity.

In 2007, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake in a province of the Ica region left nearly 600 people dead.
