World.title: From C5 to C6: how Azerbaijan is reshaping balance of power in Central Asia
World.content:
Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

On 16 November 2025, the five Central Asian states accepted Azerbaijan as a full member of the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State. Eight months later, on 31 July, Ilham Aliyev took his place at the table at an informal summit in Cholpon-Ata not as a guest, but as one of six equal participants.

The format is now officially known as “Central Asia and Azerbaijan”. The term “C6” has already entered expert vocabulary and is being used at conferences.

The change expands Central Asia’s political and economic cooperation to the western shore of the Caspian Sea. It also turns Azerbaijan from an external partner into a full participant in a route connecting the region with Turkey and Europe.

How did the format emerge and why has it expanded?

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the idea of a consultative mechanism at the UN in September 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana on 15 March 2018. The format’s advantage was its simplicity: without a treaty, permanent secretariat or supranational bodies, the leaders of the five countries could directly discuss borders, water resources, trade and security.

Azerbaijan did not join the process immediately. Ilham Aliyev attended meetings in Dushanbe in 2023, Astana in 2024 and Tashkent in 2025 as an honorary guest. Since the beginning of 2023, he has visited Central Asian countries 16 times, while the region’s leaders have travelled to Azerbaijan 26 times. In 2025, Azerbaijan’s trade with the five Central Asian states grew by 53% to $1.8 billion. Trade among the Central Asian countries themselves reached $10.7 billion in 2024.

Mirziyoyev described Baku’s accession as an opportunity to create a “single space for cooperation” between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Aliyev, in turn, described the two shores of the Caspian as a “single geopolitical and geoeconomic space”.

The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan said they supported expanding the format because it would create new opportunities for transit, logistics and energy cooperation.

The Middle Corridor and the Caspian’s role in bringing the region together

The geography offers the clearest explanation for Azerbaijan’s participation in the format. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with Europe: goods travel by rail across Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, then across the Caspian Sea to Alat, before continuing through Georgia towards Turkey and the Black Sea. Azerbaijan effectively serves as the western gateway to the route.

According to the Kazakh government, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian route rose by 62% in 2024 to 4.5 million tonnes. Baku says the volume of cargo travelling through the Azerbaijani section of the Middle Corridor has increased by 90% over three years. The authorities plan to raise the capacity of the Port of Alat to 25 million tonnes a year. The World Bank estimates that if countries coordinate border procedures, tariffs, port operations and transport schedules, freight volumes along the corridor could triple by 2030, while delivery times could fall by half.

The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Azerbaijan issues caution to citizens regarding foreign investment platforms
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. A monitoring effort conducted by the Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan has revealed that certain foreign investment platforms are promoting themselves in Azerbaijan through various means and attracting the country’s residents to use their services.

This was announced in a statement published by the press service of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan.

Meanwhile, it is noted that the services of these platforms are offered and promoted through websites, social media, educational programs, seminars, and other marketing tools.

The Central Bank states that holding a license issued by regulatory authorities in foreign countries does not grant a platform the right to provide investment services or promote them within the territory of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

“In accordance with the legislation of the Republic of Azerbaijan, investment services may be provided within the country only on the basis of a relevant license issued by the Central Bank. Before using any investment services, it is important to verify that the service provider holds the appropriate license to operate in the Republic of Azerbaijan.”

To protect investors’ rights in accordance with the law, the Central Bank recommends that citizens entrust their investments only to entities that hold an investment license issued by the Central Bank. A list of investment companies licensed by the Central Bank is available on the Central Bank’s official website (https://www.cbar.az/page-200/investment-companies).

World.title: UK ambassador highlights Azerbaijan as important economic partner
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Azerbaijan is an important economic partner for the United Kingdom, UK Ambassador to country, Duncan Norman said at a press conference in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

“Delivering economic growth is a priority for this Government. Azerbaijan is an important economic partner. We are supporting the next chapter of economic cooperation with deeper ties on trade, investment, and regional connectivity. This fosters a stable and prosperous economic environment for generations to come bringing benefits for British and Azerbaijani people and businesses,” the ambassador said.

Norman noted that energy has been the foundation of UK-Azerbaijan relations since BP entered the Azerbaijani market three decades ago. “We are proud of that legacy,” he said.

According to the ambassador, the two countries are working closely to support the energy transition. He added that the UK is investing in clean energy and contributing to the development of Azerbaijan’s renewable energy capacity.

“Beyond energy, British companies are active across several other areas. We see Azerbaijan as the natural hub for connectivity on transport, infrastructure, finance and data in this region.” Norman said.

World.title: UK values Azerbaijan as important regional partner – ambassador
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. The United Kingdom values Azerbaijan as an important regional partner, and London is committed to further developing this partnership, UK Ambassador to Azerbaijan Duncan Norman said at a press conference in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports.

“UK values Azerbaijan as an important regional partner, and I am determined to see that partnership grow,” Norman said.

He noted that cooperation between the UK and Azerbaijan has a history spanning more than 30 years. “This relationship began in energy. BP's pioneering investment helped shape Azerbaijan's modern economic story, and we are still building on that strong start,” the ambassador said.

According to Norman, bilateral cooperation has now expanded well beyond the energy sector.

“Today it spans defence, security, trade, education, innovation, and people-to-people ties that run deep on both sides. Azerbaijan is a valued partner, united by strong ties and a shared outlook on today's key challenges and opportunities.” he noted.

The ambassador added that this is why the governments of the two countries have agreed to elevate their relationship to a Strategic Partnership.

“It will drive deeper cooperation across our shared priorities: unlocking new economic growth, strengthening security and driving innovation. Together, the UK and Azerbaijan are building a shared future that delivers real benefits for Azerbaijanis and British people alike.,” Norman said.

World.title: Azerbaijani MP calls for apology from states with colonial past
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Countries with a colonial past must apologize, Azerbaijani MP Nizami Safarov said, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Safarov made the announcement at an international conference on “Belgium’s colonial injustice and 101-year path to reparations.”

“It is my firm belief that countries with a colonial past that have committed crimes against humanity and genocide in the past must apologize. This is a legal issue,” the MP said.

Moreover, Safarov noted that colonialism is a complex issue with political, legal, economic, and socio-humanitarian aspects. According to him, one of the fundamental issues from a legal standpoint is the legal characterization of acts committed during the colonial period.

“Undoubtedly, the actions and crimes committed by certain states can be classified in only one way: as crimes against humanity,” he emphasized.

The lawmaker stated that the concept of crimes against humanity emerged in connection with the transatlantic slave trade, and this term was reflected in a number of articles published by American universities in the mid-19th century.

According to him, there are also important legal precedents for classifying crimes committed during the colonial period as crimes against humanity.

N. Safarov drew attention to the ruling of the Brussels Court of Appeals in this context. He noted that the court classified the separation of mixed-race children from their families, their relocation to other places, as well as their discrimination and segregation by the Belgian authorities during the colonial period as a crime against humanity.

“This is a very important symbolic ruling that holds great significance as a groundbreaking legal precedent,” the MP said.

Nizami Safarov also addressed the issue of the right of victims of colonialism to compensation. He recalled that the draft articles of the UN Commission on International Law on the Responsibility of States for Acts Contrary to International Law provide for compensation, restitution, and reparations.

According to the MP, since restitution implies restoring the previous situation, this is impossible in many cases involving acts committed during the colonial period. Therefore, the issues of damages and compensation are of particular importance.

He emphasized that satisfaction entails an apology from the state that committed the act contrary to international law, whereas compensation entails financial compensation for the damage caused.

World.title: Tajikistan calls timely completion of Rogun HPP vital for energy future
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. The timely completion of the Rogun Hydropower Plant and the full commissioning of its capacity are vital for Tajikistan.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Tajik president, citing President Rahmon's remarks made at a meeting with employees working in the construction of the Rogun HPP.

“By building and commissioning Rogun, we are ensuring the prosperous present and bright future of our beloved homeland – Tajikistan – as well as a happy life for present and future generations,” Rahmon said.

He noted that amid current global conditions, energy security has become one of the key objectives for states. According to the president, each completed stage of the Rogun HPP project brings Tajikistan closer to its strategic national goal of achieving full energy independence and developing a green economy.

Rahmon also stressed the need to comply with international quality and safety standards during construction. “Any deviation from quality and safety requirements is unacceptable at such a unique project of the century,” the president said. Rahmon described Rogun HPP as the country's largest hydropower project and one of the world's highest dams. He stressed that its stability, reliability and safety must therefore be fully ensured.

Meanwhile, the Rogun Hydropower Plant is being built on the Vakhsh River in southern Tajikistan and is one of the country's largest infrastructure projects. Once completed, the facility is planned to have an installed capacity of 3,780 megawatts.

The project includes the construction of a 335-meter-high rockfill dam, which is expected to become the world's tallest of its kind. The dam and reservoir are being developed in complex mountainous and underground geological conditions, requiring large-scale excavation, tunneling, and construction works.

Rogun HPP is intended to increase Tajikistan's electricity generation capacity and improve the country's energy security, while also creating additional potential for electricity exports to regional markets.

Construction of the plant has been carried out in stages, with work focusing on the dam, underground structures, tunnels and reservoir. The project remains a major priority for the Tajik government as the country seeks to expand its hydropower capacity and strengthen its energy infrastructure.

World.title: Azerbaijani MP highlights importance of recognition of Belgium’s colonial history
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Belgian colonial policy in Central Africa has had profound consequences that are still felt today and, therefore, acknowledging historical injustices is a necessary prerequisite for building a more just future, Azerbaijani MP Tural Ganjaliyev said, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Ganjaliyev made the remarks at an international conference in Baku on “Belgium’s colonial injustice and 101-year path to reparations.”

He noted that Belgium’s more than century-long colonial rule in Central Africa, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda and Burundi, left lasting consequences, including systematic economic exploitation, widespread violence, and the destruction of local societies and institutions. “Recognizing the past is a necessary condition for building a more just future,” Ganjaliyev said.

According to him, these historical facts are not a matter of opinion, but are documented and recognized by numerous researchers, legal experts and international institutions. “These facts are not a matter of opinion. They are documented history, recognized by numerous researchers, legal experts and international institutions,” he noted.

Furthermore, Ganjaliyev stressed that the discussion should now focus not on whether historical injustice took place, but on how the international community, the states concerned and Belgium itself can move toward its full recognition and concrete reparations. “This includes such forms of redress as restitution, compensation and guarantees of non-recurrence,” the MP said.

The MP noted that the Baku conference brought together representatives of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Morocco and South Africa, along with various African perspectives united by a common call for historical justice.

in addition, Ganjaliyev emphasized the importance of conducting a historical and legal assessment of Belgium’s colonial period and discussing concrete legal mechanisms that could pave the way for reparations.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s Uzbekneftegaz, China’s CCDC set key priority areas for co-op
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Uzbekistan’s Uzbekneftegaz and China’s CCDC have identified four priority areas for cooperation aimed at improving oil and gas production efficiency through advanced technologies and pilot projects.

This was announced in a stetement by the press service of the Uzbekneftgaz.

According to Uzbekneftegaz, in the course of the meeting, the sides reviewed the current state of their cooperation, existing challenges in production processes and opportunities to address them using CCDC’s modern technologies and expertise

The four priority areas are drilling and its digitalization, improving gas recovery from fields, geological exploration and engineering and design.

The sides also considered opportunities to launch pilot projects at Uzbekneftegaz facilities in each of the four areas.

“Pilot projects will allow the technologies proposed by CCDC to be tested under the specific geological and production conditions of Uzbekistan’s fields and their efficiency and applicability to be assessed,” Uzbekneftegaz said.

The company emphasized that cooperation should go beyond simply presenting new technologies and instead focus on adapting them to specific production challenges.

Under the proposed approach, technologies would be introduced gradually through pilot projects, allowing the sides to assess their practical results before considering broader deployment.

The digitalization of drilling operations could help improve the management and efficiency of drilling activities, while measures to increase gas recovery could support more effective use of existing fields.

Geological exploration was identified as another priority, potentially supporting more accurate assessments of Uzbekistan’s resource base and the identification of new development opportunities.

The engineering and design component could also help improve the preparation and implementation of oil and gas projects through the use of modern technical solutions.

The sides expect the pilot projects to provide a practical basis for evaluating CCDC technologies and determining which solutions can be scaled across Uzbekneftegaz operations.

The approach is intended to establish a long-term and mutually beneficial partnership between Uzbekneftegaz and CCDC while improving oil and gas production efficiency through the adoption of advanced technologies.

The cooperation also reflects Uzbekistan’s broader efforts to modernize its energy sector, increase the efficiency of domestic hydrocarbon production and introduce digital and technology-driven solutions into industrial operations.

World.title: Ex-minister threatens legal action over 'slanderous' comments
World.content:
Former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott has said he will take legal action against those he believes have said "slanderous things" about him, following a corruption watchdog hearing.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining whether donations linked to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including attempts to damage Mr Elliott's career.

On Friday, the former police minister gave evidence to ICAC.

After taking the stand, Mr Elliott told reporters outside that he would be talking to his lawyer about taking legal action against those he believed "need to be pursued", but stopped short of naming anyone specifically.

He said the "battle" of fighting corruption in the parliament was not over, and claimed there were still people in the Liberal shadow ministry "who gave evidence to criminals".

"We still have people in that parliamentary party, in the NSW parliament who were a party to the corruption that we've seen not only today but over the last month," Mr Elliott said.

Mr Elliott said the fight against corruption in NSW parliament "was not over". (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

The ICAC previously heard allegations that senior Liberal MPs Chris Rath and Damien Tudehope remained in contact with people trying to avoid giving evidence to a 2023 parliamentary inquiry.

Mr Rath allegedly helped lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood stay informed about efforts to serve him with a summons, while Mr Tudehope was accused of passing a confidential committee report to Mr Greenwood.

Mr Tudehope has not been accused of wrongdoing, while Mr Greenwood and other persons of interest in the inquiry have not been charged with any crimes.

Surveillance photos 'very creepy'

Mr Elliott told the inquiry he now believed Mr Nassif influenced the decision to remove him as police minister in a 2021 cabinet reshuffle.

Mr Elliott linked the move to Mr Nassif's 2019 arrest for cocaine possession at The Star casino, saying the developer may have blamed him for police being at the casino.

"I think Nassif had probably made it clear to the hard-right that because he'd got arrested for cocaine, that I wasn't to be trusted with the police force," Mr Elliott said.

Mr Elliott told the inquiry that he believed Mr Nassif was behind a campaign against him. (Background Briefing: Cherine Yazbeck, file photo)

The inquiry previously heard NSW Liberal Party operatives allegedly compiled a "David Elliott shit sheet" — a dossier of political and personal allegations aimed at damaging his career.

Mr Elliott told ICAC he believed Mr Nassif was behind a campaign of negative media stories against him, after he responded to community concerns about one of his developments.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Mr Elliott said Mr Nassif later confronted him twice and left a message on his phone threatening to "get" him.

He also told the inquiry private investigators followed him and his wife, describing surveillance images of his wife as "very creepy".

Mr Elliott said Mr Nassif allegedly pressured his former chief of staff to provide information about him and warned that his political career could be over.

Mr Elliott ultimately decided not to seek Liberal preselection for Castle Hill because he said branch-stacking had made it clear the seat would go to a candidate from the party's "religious right".

Asked about his characterisation of the factions within the NSW Liberal Party, Mr Elliott said: "Depending on who you're talking to, some call it the hard right, some call it the right, some call it the religious right, some call it the cult."

World.title: Israel open to compensating Zomi Frankcom's family, ambassador says
World.content:
Israel's ambassador to Australia has suggested reparations could be available for the family of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

This week the Israel Defense Forces cleared soldiers of criminal liability for their involvement in the April 2024 strike in Gaza that killed Ms Frankcom and six of her World Central Kitchen colleagues.

The move has outraged the Australian government, which slammed the findings and demanded an apology for Ms Frankcom's family.

Ambassador Hillel Newman, who has defiantly defended the IDF probe, was hauled into a meeting with Foreign Minister Penny Wong at Parliament House on Thursday.

Wong has 'no confidence' in IDF report Foreign Minister Penny Wong says she has 'no confidence' in the IDF investigation that cleared Israeli soldiers of criminal wrongdoing in the killing of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom.

On Friday Mr Newman again declined to apologise but expressed sorrow for the family and left the door open to reparations.

"Reparations is an issue that we can check and will be checked by Israel. It's not my decision here in Australia," Mr Newman told Radio National.

"We need a specific request and then it's investigated according to the rules of reparations in such cases.

"The issue of sorrow and grief of the family has been expressed personally and generally, very categorically."

The report cleared the soldiers involved in the strikes that killed Zomi Frankcom and six other aid workers. (Supplied: X)

On Thursday Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said further investigation of the killings was "one of the options" that should be considered, but would not reveal the Australian government's next moves.

"We will press the Israeli government," he told the ABC's 7.30.

"The direction, we have said today, we'll discuss with Ms Frankcom's family.

"They deserve to be consulted on these issues, and we'll do that and then we'll make an announcement in coming days."

Mr Newman said Israel was open to possible legal avenues for further investigation.

In 2024 Senator Wong appointed Air Chief Marshal Mark Binskin to investigate Israel's response to the strikes.

His report found that the killings were a result of serious failures to follow IDF procedures and errors in decision-making. The report was in line with the IDF's finding that the incident was a "grave mistake".

The report also called for reparations and an apology from the Israeli government.

Israel did not grant Air Chief Marshal Binskin access to the audio from the drone attack in question.

Anthony Albanese says Australia will continue to demand answers from Israel. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

On Thursday Mr Albanese said there needed to be a "far more transparent and clear explanation" from the Israeli government about what had occurred and called for the audio to be released.

"That's consistent with transparency, which is something we have called for from day one," he said.

Mr Newman said he was not privy to intelligence regarding the recording and would not commit to its release.

"I don't think that Australia shares all its intelligence aspects with other nations, even if they're friendly and they're like-minded," he said.

"That is a question which is up to security agencies."

Mr Newman also said Israel was considering inviting Air Chief Marshal Binskin back to the country for further talks.

The Frankcom family has expressed deep disappointment over the decision to clear the soldiers involved in the strike.

They also said it was an insult to Ms Frankcom's memory for the findings to be announced on World Humanitarian Day.

IDF clears soldiers over 2024 Gaza WCK strike Penny Wong said she is "outraged" and plans to haul in the Israeli ambassador after the Israel Defense Forces cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing in the April 2024 strike on a World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza, where Australian woman Zomi Frankcom was killed.

The prime minister also expressed frustration with the timing of the report's release.

"It's certainly not good enough that, on World Humanitarian Day, of all days, they release this so-called report that essentially says, 'Yes, we're responsible, but nothing to see here,'" Mr Albanese said.

Mr Newman said he and the Israeli government had been under pressure to release the findings.

"It could be that the timing was not good," he said.

The IDF investigation found that there were "serious failures" in the strike, but they did not raise "reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct".

The findings released by Israel on Wednesday also looked into four other high-profile civilian deaths in Gaza.

Israel has opened criminal investigations into two of the cases, including the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza in January 2025.

World.title: Five people in ACT die from suspected overdoses in a fortnight
World.content:
Five people in the ACT have died from suspected drug overdoses in the past fortnight alone, prompting a warning from health and emergency services about the presence of potentially lethal drugs circulating the territory.

Another two people survived reported drug overdoses in the last week, ACT Policing said.

Officers suspect opioids were involved in all cases.

"Opioids obviously carry a high level of addiction, and our message to drug users and those around them is to be aware of the signs of an overdose," Detective Superintendent Peta Lankester said.

" Obviously we are investigating each of the incidents and the coroner will determine the outcome for each of those. "

Directions Health Services CEO Bronwyn Hendry held a press conference after a concerning number of deaths due to suspected overdose. (ABC News: Jade Toomey)

'Not realising what they can do'

In the past year, 25 people in Canberra have died from suspected drug overdoses, police said.

Health officials said some drug overdoses could be attributed to online purchases of imitation prescription drugs by unsuspecting users.

"They're tainted, or they're just not realising what they can do; they're often not what they purport to be," Bronwyn Hendry from Directions Health Services said.

"They're buying oxycodone or they're buying benzodiazepine in some form or another … and the drug doesn't turn out to be that.

" We know very little about a lot of those things that turn up. "

Bronwyn Hendry was joined by ACT Policing North District Detective Superintendent Peta Lankester and paramedic Sam Perillo to warn the public about opioids. (ABC News: Jade Toomey)

Directions Health Services, the agency behind CanTEST, is the only publicly available drug-testing clinic in the country, located in Canberra.

Recent test results have triggered serious concern.

"We found heroin in cocaine a couple of times recently," Ms Hendry said.

"But, unfortunately, now we've got nitazenes that have crept into the illicit drug market, and they're worse than fentanyl.

"It can be up to a thousand times stronger than morphine, for example."

Nitazenes, a strong synthetic opioid, are not a prescribed pharmaceutical drug but could potentially be imported from overseas markets, Ms Hendry warned.

Public warned to intervene early

ACT Ambulance said while the recent cluster of deaths was concerning, they had not resulted in an increased workload for paramedics.

"If you are concerned, don't wait, intervene early and call us as soon as you can," paramedic Sam Perillo from the Clinical Governance Unit said.

"Use naloxone if you have it, that's the best way to intervene early."

Naloxone can be used as part of the emergency treatment of an overdose. (ABC News: Jade Toomey)

Naloxone is a nasal spray administered up someone's nostrils and can rapidly reverse the effects of an overdose.

It is free at CanTEST, CAHMA, Woden Needle and Syringe Programs and select pharmacies.

The ACT Coroner will investigate the cause of the five recent deaths.

World.title: Australia names team for second Test against Bangladesh
World.content:
Australia have resisted the temptation to play four specialist fast bowlers against Bangladesh in the second Test in Mackay, as captain Pat Cummins confirmed Matt Renshaw would open the batting.

The recalled Renshaw is a straight swap for Jake Weatherald, who was dropped after six underwhelming Test matches.

The pitch at Great Barrier Reef Arena is expected to assist the pacemen, but off spinner Nathan Lyon, after taking 1-102 in the first innings of the nine-wicket loss by Australia in Darwin, will play his 143rd Test.

Australia vs Bangladesh second Test preview Winter cricket continues in the Top End, with Australia looking for a big response in the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay.

Outstanding paceman Scott Boland did not play in Darwin and will now have to wait until the tour of South Africa in October for his next Test, after starring in last summer's Ashes.

Pitch curator Peter Kazakoff said the Mackay wicket would suit fast bowlers on both sides.

"That is what we are aiming for, a lot of pace," he said.

"We want the ball to come through really nicely. We have got the same sort of clay as the Gabba, so we are expecting similar sort of characteristics to that."

Australia confirmed their side, with Lyon in it, an hour after captain Cummins held a press conference where he said he was considering an all-out pace attack.

Kazakoff said there would be a role for Lyon and the Bangladesh spinners.

"I think the spinners will come into the game, going off previous first-class games here," he said.

"Spinners have had a big say later in the match. Obviously those first-class games were a bit later in the year when it was a bit warmer.

"It is a lot cooler this time of year. The moisture will come out of the wicket less and slower."

There has been a lot of talk about "soul-searching" in the Australian camp after the Darwin loss, but Cummins said he was confident of a response.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"In home Test matches we pride ourselves on winning as many as we can," he said.

"It's funny. I think if we played really well and we lost you'd feel like we needed to do some soul-searching.

"I certainly felt like we didn't play anywhere near our best and they played really well. When we play well, fortunately we have got a decent body of work to look back on."

Weatherald's axing was simple to explain for Cummins, who said he was "awesome around the group" but did not deliver.

"Over the course of six Test matches he didn't quite score the runs he or we would have liked," Cummins said.

Renshaw, 30, will play his first Test in three years after averaging 49.9 in Sheffield Shield cricket last summer, including scoring three centuries.

"[Renshaw] has been really impressive and had some great off-season tours of Pakistan and Bangladesh recently with white-ball (formats). He looks in good nick," Cummins said.

"He had a really good Shield season last season.

"Some of the kind of chat about [Renshaw] in the past is that he can look different from day to day.

"When you get to the back half of your career as a batter you want to really know what you look like at your best, and I think he does that.

"I hope he brings his best version every day, is nice and sharp and puts the pressure on the bowlers."

Australia XI for second Test: Matthew Renshaw, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey (wk), Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (c), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood

World.title: Commissioner says Kumanjayi Little Baby case will 'stay with you forever'
World.content:
The Northern Territory's most senior police officer has described the investigation into the alleged murder of five-year-old girl Kumanjayi Little Baby as "one of the most difficult investigations" officers had ever faced.

Speaking at this year's NT Police Association (NTPA) conference in Darwin, Commissioner Martin Dole acknowledged the "challenging" year officers had faced across the territory.

The past eight months have been marred by devastating flooding across vast swathes of the Top End, unrest in remote communities and several horrific highway fatalities — including one crash that claimed five lives earlier this month.

Martin Dole says the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby is a moment that will stay with police forever. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Commissioner Dole also highlighted the "incredibly difficult circumstances" police faced following the tragic death of Kumanjayi Little Baby in Alice Springs in April, which saw violent riots erupt after the arrest of her alleged killer.

"I want to acknowledge one of the most difficult investigations some of our officers have ever experienced with the search for Kumanjayi Little Baby, the apprehension of the [alleged] offender … and then the fallout after that apprehension," he said.

"There are moments in policing that stay with you forever and that was one of them for many of our people.

"The officers, investigators, specialist units and partner agencies involved showed extraordinary professionalism, compassion and resilience."

Morale, attrition priorities

Wellbeing was a theme of this year's conference with NTPA president Nathan Finn noting remote policing remained one of the "most significant workplaces challenges" for the force.

Kumanjayi Little Baby remembered at funeral service Hundreds of members of the Alice Springs community have turned out dressed in pink to mourn Kumanjayi Little Baby at her funeral today.

'"If government expects experienced police officers to move their families, commit to remote communities and remain there … it must provide safe housing, adequate staffing, reliable infrastructure and incentives that recognise the genuine demands of remote service in the NT," he said.

Less than a week ago, police in the remote community of Wadeye were allegedly attacked by a large group of men armed with arrows, rocks, metal bars and window louvres following weeks of unrest in the area.

Mr Finn thanked the NT government for coming to the table on the latest industrial agreement but said pay rises alone would not effectively reduce attrition rates.

The conference heard vacancy rates were as high as 60 per cent in some remote areas.

"The real question is whether an experienced officer can look at a career in the Northern Territory and see something worth staying for," he said.

Lia Finocchiaro says attrition rates are improving but there is still work to be done. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

In her address, Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro noted the overall attrition rate had dropped from 10.7 per cent in 2022 to 7.1 per cent in 2026 but said more work needed to be done.

"More people are joining and fewer are leaving," she said.

"But that number needs to be much lower."

Police feel weight of CLP policies

Mr Finn also noted police had carried a "significant share of the responsibility" for delivering the NT Country Liberal Party (CLP) government's crime reduction strategy, which has seen an increase in the number of arrests during the past year.

He said the use of police watch houses as longer-term detention facilities had placed added pressure on an already stretched workforce.

Nathan Finn says watch houses should be "used for policing purpose for which they are designed". (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"The NTPA will continue to insist that police watch houses are properly staffed, properly resourced and used for policing purpose for which they are designed," he said.

" Pressure in one part of the justice system can't simply be transferred to police and re-labelled as someone else's workload. "

Mrs Finocchiaro said the government had "cleared" police watch houses and spruiked a recent announcement to build a privately-operated, 1,200-bed prison which she said would ensure police "never ever have overflowing watch houses ever again".

World.title: Man jailed for chainsaw torment of teenager in shipping container
World.content:
A Tasmanian man who left a teenager tied up in a locked shipping container, threatened him with a chainsaw to his neck and later told the boy's father, "you'll never see your son again" if supposedly stolen items weren't returned, a court has heard.

WARNING: This story contains details of violence that some readers may find distressing

On Friday, Wayne Michael Ludbey, 32, was jailed for what the judge described as "premeditated violence carried out for vindictive reasons".

Ludbey pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Tasmania in Burnie to two counts of assault for the 2023 attack on the 17-year-old, which started around midday on September 12.

During sentencing, Justice Tamara Jago said that, despite the guilty plea, she did not accept that Ludbey had demonstrated remorse or shown insight into the seriousness of his crimes.

Boy restrained, bashed, sprayed with hose

The court heard that Ludbey believed the teenager had been stealing from the shipping container on his property at Strahan on Tasmania's West Coast.

Justice Jago told the court that on the day, Ludbey saw the boy and believed he was wearing work boots stolen from the container.

Ludbey then texted his wife: "I'm waiting for him, I'm going to get him".

About half an hour later, Ludbey confronted the teenager on the street and began assaulting him and attempted to force him into his nearby vehicle.

Ludbey saw the boy walking in Strahan on the day of the incident, the court heard. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Ludbey's younger brother Brady Ludbey then joined him in the attack, helping force the teenager into the car and allowing his elder brother to return to the driver's seat.

The younger brother was previously sentenced for his lesser part in the assault.

Justice Jago told the court Ludbey then drove the teenager to his property, accused him of the theft and demanded that his belongings be returned.

"The complainant had no idea what you were talking about, nor why you were accusing him," the judge said.

Brothers who kidnapped, menaced teen with chainsaw lashed by judge A teenage boy was "terrified" during an assault by two brothers, during which he was kidnapped and menaced with a chainsaw in a shipping container in Tasmania.

At the shipping container, the assault continued and the Ludbey brothers restrained the teenager with straps and zip ties bound around his hands and legs.

Ludbey then started a chainsaw, revved it, and held the chain against the boy's neck while it was not moving.

He then bashed the boy with a piece of wood to his arms and head, causing several injuries.

After spraying the boy with a hose, Ludbey and his younger brother locked the container with a chain and padlock, leaving the boy tied up inside.

"You left him trapped, wet, restrained and undoubtedly very frightened," Justice Jago said.

The judge said a short time later that Ludbey, who had possession of the boy's phone, called the boy's father from it and issued the ultimatum about returning his possessions.

"You said, 'I want my stuff back or you'll never see your son again'," Justice Jago said.

"You were prepared to utter emotional threats to the complainant's father.

" Your conduct was disgraceful. "

A short time later, Brady Ludbey freed the boy from the container, returned his phone and told him to go home.

The boy was taken to hospital with minor physical injuries, but Justice Jago said she had no doubt the psychological harm was "significant" and that he would have been "deeply traumatised".

Justice Jago told the court that Ludbey had not shown remorse. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Judge lashes man for 'lack of insight'

At the outset of proceedings, defence lawyer Greg Richardson said it was his "privilege" to provide the court with 49 separate character references from people who supported Ludbey.

Justice Jago, however, said she found it "difficult to reconcile" the letters praising Ludbey's character with his "egregious behaviour".

She said that generally, people who are described as pillars of their community "do not behave in this way", although his character was supported by the fact he had not committed similar crimes before or since the attack.

However, she said Ludbey had not shown remorse and had demonstrated "a serious lack of insight into the gravity" of his crimes.

"This was premeditated violence carried out for vindictive reasons," the judge said.

She sentenced Ludbey to 14 months' jail, of which 10 months were suspended for two years.

In court, Ludbey was supported by more than a dozen people, several of whom became emotional when he was jailed.

World.title: 'Career destroying': AFP officer jailed for lying about evidence
World.content:
A senior Australian Federal Police (AFP) detective who admitted to lying under oath about evidence seized during a criminal investigation will spend four months behind bars.

Trent Madders, 52, had pleaded guilty to a count of perjury, in that he knowingly made false statements in legal proceedings in August 2020.

In handing down his sentence in the ACT Supreme Court, Justice David Mossop said Madders's conduct reflected a "tragic misjudgement".

"The perjury was career destroying … and much more serious than the conduct it was trying to hide," Justice Mossop said.

He said Madders undermined the "proper administration of justice" and had an impact on the perception of police being honest and reliable.

Case centres around evidence seized

Madders was the officer in charge of the 2019 investigation into identical twin brothers Joshua, who was also an AFP officer, and Kenan Tiffen, who were accused of secretly filming female tenants at a Canberra property they owned.

During the investigation, police seized a mobile phone and laptop which were required to be examined within 30 days unless an extension was granted.

Madders did not seek an extension and was later told by AFP digital forensics staff that the devices had not been examined within the required time-frame.

Madders admitted his offending was the "dumbest thing he's ever done". (Supplied)

But when the admissibility of the evidence was challenged in the ACT Magistrates Court in 2020, Madders gave sworn evidence that he had been assured the devices had been examined in time.

He maintained that account under cross-examination despite being confronted with emails showing otherwise, and has since admitted those statements were knowingly false.

The Tiffen brothers were initially found guilty in 2022, but successfully appealed their convictions after evidence obtained from the laptop was ruled unlawful.

The case was sent back to the ACT Magistrates Court and the brothers were found guilty again in September 2025 of attempting to capture indecent visual data.

Lies were 'deliberately told': prosecution

Prosecutor Keegan Lee argued Madders's lies were "deliberately told, repeated and maintained".

"This is an offence that strikes at the heart of the administration of justice," he told the court.

" This is not a minor or momentary lapse of judgement. "

Defence barrister Beth Morrisroe said Madders admitted his offending was the "dumbest thing he has ever done".

"He is remorseful, he has demonstrated insight … he has taken accountability," she said.

She described Madders as an "overworked" officer who was experiencing significant stress, pressure and fatigue.

The judge described Madders's offending as a "tragic misjudgement". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Due to his time in the police force in the ACT, the court heard it was likely he would need to be transferred to a "far away" New South Wales correctional facility if a jail sentence was imposed.

But Ms Morrisroe argued he would be exposed to a "heightened level of risk" in any prison due to the national media attention he received through his involvement in investigating Brittany Higgins's rape allegation.

Justice Mossop sentenced him to almost a year in prison, to be suspended after four months, after which he will be subject to a good behaviour order.

Madders has been suspended from duty with the AFP since he was charged in 2024.

In a statement, the AFP said Madders was still subject to an internal investigation into his conduct.

World.title: ‘Justice will prevail’: Ex military man David Elliott uses ICAC to machine gun opponents
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny ‘Justice will prevail’: Ex military man David Elliott uses ICAC to machine gun opponents Kate McClymont August 21, 2026 — 5:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Marching down Elizabeth Street, his silk regimental tie from Duntroon military college tucked neatly into his charcoal suit, former army officer and ex-Liberal minister David Elliott presented a stark contrast to the parade of reluctant witnesses who have arrived at the ICAC over the past month. David Elliott arrives at the ICAC on Friday. Peter Rae “Justice will prevail!” he said enthusiastically to the cameras before catching the lift to the 7th floor of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s hearing room. David Andrew Elliott, who had eight portfolios during his time in parliament, declined the offer of a “Section 38” declaration, which effectively ensures the evidence you give before the ICAC can’t be used against you in future proceedings, unless you are caught lying. Elliott was taken through the role played by fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, along with members of the Opus Dei “religious right” as Elliot described them, in attempting to topple him.



Nassif felt that Elliott, as the local member, was blocking his developments. Nassif, who is wanted for serious fraud charges, fled to Lebanon in December 2022 on the eve of a NSW parliamentary inquiry examining similar matters to the ICAC inquiry. Several months later, Toplace, Nassif’s development and construction company, collapsed with debts of around $1.6 billion. Christian Ellis and Jean Nassif. Supllied. The commission heard that on two occasions, Nassif confronted Elliott – once in Elliott’s local shopping centre and once in a Parramatta pub. He also left a threat on his phone and hired a private investigator to spy on Elliott.



“He was the Maxwell Smart of the private investigators,” Elliott said of the efforts of Nassif’s private eye Shane De Kauwe. “Missed it by that much,” accompanied by his thumb and forefinger close together, was the famous catch phrase of the hapless fictional television detective upon failing yet another assignment. Shane De Kauwe, the private investigator hired by fugitive developer Jean Nassif. It seemed Nassif’s PI also missed it by that much, having targeted the wrong house and the wrong car, according to Elliott. The former army officer took every chance to fire off shots at those whom he felt had wronged him. The Perrottet brothers were the prime target.



One of the allegations the commission is investigating is whether Nassif, a prohibited donor, funnelled money to right-wing Liberal operatives Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet, brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet. In return, Nassif wanted people such as Elliott and then-building commissioner David Chandler out of the way and for public officials more amenable to his developments to be appointed to positions of power. Describing Charles Perrottet as the “muscle” in his brother’s government, Elliott said Charles “did the dirty work” and was pulling the strings for his brother’s Right faction. Also in Elliott’s line of fire was Dallas McInerney, the once-powerful factional leader of the Right of the party, whom Elliott described as “duplicitous”. While Elliott was giving evidence, it was revealed Catholic Schools NSW had sacked McInerney, its long-term CEO.



“Due Diligence” Dallas, as he was known, had a torrid time in the witness box earlier in the week when he revealed – to the astonishment of counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC – that he had effectively wiped his phone and iPad by doing a factory reset on both. There hasn’t been as much publicity about a factory reset since the trial of now-convicted mushroom killer Erin Patterson, who wiped her phone clean by doing a factory reset while police were executing a search warrant at her house. Dwyer suggested it was a “transparent attempt to wipe evidence”, which McInerney denied, saying it was because he’d been informed by his bank that his account had been compromised. Dallas McInerney said he wiped his devices over the weekend. Michael Howard In his earlier evidence, McInerney had made much of the “due diligence” he’d undertaken by hiring Ellis and Greenwood, who had established lobbying firm Beckington. It is alleged Beckington used money from Nassif and Catholic Schools NSW to fund Liberal branch stacking.



McInerney claimed to have done months of due diligence before agreeing that Catholic Schools NSW would be the first clients of Beckington. Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Catholic Schools NSW sacks Dallas McInerney, former police minister gives evidence However, he failed to discover Ellis’ most recent boss, Liberal MP Damien Tudehope, had fired Ellis. But McInerney assured the commission he had checked with then premier Dominic Perrottet. “So what information were you getting from Mr Perrottet by way of due diligence?” he was asked. He said the premier’s response was “favourable” and “he knew both of the individuals”. However, when Dwyer asked Elliott whether he’d ever heard the name “Christian Ellis” before the current allegations were raised, Elliott replied only once and that was when “Dominic [Perrottet] just absolutely sledged him because he had to sack him”.



Ellis had been employed as a staffer but was sacked when Perrottet found a pile of unanswered correspondence from constituents, Elliott said. Ellis, who has moved to England, has said he is unable to assist the inquiry due to the time difference and family commitments.

World.title: A sacked CEO, a bungling detective and a jar of fingers: Five things we learnt from Operation Rosny week four
World.content:
See what we learnt from week three of Operation Rosny here. A three-day week of evidence at the ICAC began with revelations former Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney had wiped his phone and iPad at a pub over the weekend and ended with an unscheduled press conference by an impassioned former police minister David Elliott on the street outside the commission’s CBD base. Here are five things we learnt. 1. McInerney sacked after factory reset Move over Royal Oaks, there’s a new pub of interest to the Independent Commission Against Corruption. The Hunters Hill Hotel was the place McInerney repaired to after last week’s appearance at the inquiry into allegations of corruption.



There he discovered his bank account did not work. That was the start of a chain of events that led to him telling the ICAC on Wednesday that he had factory reset his work iPhone and iPad. Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, suggested it was a “transparent attempt to wipe evidence”, which McInerney denied. Dallas McInerney said he wiped his devices over the weekend. Michael Howard McInerney said he handed his devices back to Catholic Schools NSW because he understood it was unlikely he would be returning to work. It was a prescient observation. McInerney learnt on Friday morning he had been sacked as chief executive by the board of Catholic Schools NSW.



2. With friends like these ... Eleni Petinos, a former minister for fair trading and small business in the Perrottet government, told the ICAC she was disgusted by the thought that she was being used in a plot to remove building commissioner David Chandler from office. She told the inquiry she now believes that Chris Spence, the former chief of staff to Anthony Roberts, leant on his friendship with her to get Chandler sacked. Petinos leaves ICAC on Thursday. Ben Symons “Frankly, even the little I knew coming into here today is enough to leave me disgusted and to feel like personal relationships were leant on in a highly improper way, and that’s not someone that you would call a friend,” she said.



Petinos was herself sacked as a minister by Dominic Perrottet after bullying allegations in 2022, and appeared on the verge of tears at the inquiry while recounting the phone call in which Dominic Perrottet delivered the news. “He was very, very cold. He was immovable.” 3. The jar with fingers Petinos offered a taste of the former building commissioner David Chandler’s “robust” style in her evidence to the inquiry. Chandler, who is not a person of interest to the inquiry, was the target of a campaign by fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, who is. “Chandler had bravado about conducting meetings with [a] jar with fingers in it and putting it on tables to indicate what he would do to people if they acted outside the confines of the law.”



Former Building Commissioner David Chandler. Steven Siewert This ghoulish anecdote was not explored further, with Petinos going on to say she respected Chandler’s professional judgment and gave no serious weight to suggestions he was “dodgy”. Chandler is due to appear as a witness to the ICAC inquiry next week. Whether he brings his jar remains to be seen. 4. Private detective stalked wrong house The inquiry earlier heard evidence of an intimidation and smear campaign against former police minister David Elliott, including false assertions that Elliott was having an affair.



The false claim emerged in part from surveillance undertaken by private detective Shane De Kauwe, whom the ICAC alleges was paid by Nassif. But the one-time Australian Federal Police officer made a series of errors, including monitoring a house Elliott no longer lived in. “In hindsight, I probably should have taken more action against it,” Elliott told the ICAC. “Is it morally reprehensible for somebody to monitor a cabinet minister based on gossip and innuendo and repeat it? Yes. But you can see by the fact that he was monitoring the wrong house, I probably had very little reason to be worried.” 5. The happiest ICAC witness ever It’s fair to say Elliott enjoyed his day at the ICAC.



As well as detailing what he knew of the intimidation campaign allegedly launched at him by Nassif, he laid waste to all and sundry on Friday, calling Opus Dei a “cult” that was taking over Liberal branches, and even speculating that he was removed as police minister because Nassif was busted with cocaine at Star City Casino in 2019. All smiles: Former MP David Elliott after giving evidence on Friday. Peter Rae He gave an impromptu press conference outside the ICAC, telling reporters he would take legal action against those who had smeared him. “I must say also, it feels weird to be the first Liberal to ever be very happy to appear before ICAC.” What we expect from next week The ICAC is back on Monday, with Christopher Spence, the former chief of staff to ex-planning minister Anthony Roberts, due to give evidence. The ICAC heard claims this week that Spence leant on his friendship with Petinos to push for Chandler’s removal from office.



The inquiry is not sitting on Tuesday, but on Wednesday Anita Perrottet, wife of Charles Perrottet, is due to appear. Anita Perrottet was mentioned in the ICAC counsel assisting’s opening address as being the director of a company that received funds from Nassif. Chandler is scheduled to take the witness stand on Thursday, while Anita’s husband Charles is slated to appear on Friday. Charles Perrottet is considered a person of interest at the inquiry because the ICAC is investigating if he was involved in a plot to solicit donations from Nassif to support Liberal Party factional work, and in exchange would pursue Nassif’s interests. World.title: Catholic Schools NSW sacks Dallas McInerney, former police minister gives evidence
World.content:
Catholic Schools NSW has sacked its chief executive officer Dallas McInerney after his damaging appearance in the witness box at the Independent Commission Against Corruption, as the Catholic Church seeks to insulate itself from a growing donations scandal. Board members moved against McInerney on Friday morning as the corruption watchdog heard new details of an at-times comical campaign of surveillance and intimidation against the state’s police minister ordered at the behest of Sydney developer Jean Nassif. Dallas McInerney was identified as a target to help win a contract with the National Catholic Education Commission. Monique Westermann The intimidation and smear campaign, which is unrelated to McInerney but being explored under the same Operation Rosny inquiry, included false assertions that cabinet minister David Elliott was having an affair. The false claim emerged in part from surveillance undertaken by private detective Shane De Kauwe, whom the ICAC alleges was paid by Nassif. But the one-time Australian Federal Police officer made a series of errors, including monitoring a house Elliott no longer lived in.



“In hindsight, I probably should have taken more action against it,” Elliott told the ICAC. “Is it morally reprehensible for somebody to monitor a cabinet minister based on gossip and innuendo and repeat it? Yes. But you can see by the fact that he was monitoring the wrong house, I probably had very little reason to be worried.” David Elliott outside the ICAC on Friday. Peter Rae Earlier, Catholic Schools NSW released a statement confirming McInerney’s contract had been terminated following his appearance at the ICAC on over the past two weeks. The ICAC alleges McInerney potentially broke donation laws by directing hundreds of thousands of dollars towards a conservative Christian Liberal Party sub-faction known as the Reformers.



Related Article Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Dallas McInerney sacked as Catholic Schools NSW CEO; former NSW police minister David Elliott says Jean Nassif followed him, threatened his career McInerney told the Herald after his sacking: “When the inquiry started, I said I would privilege the position of the company before my own. That is why I stood aside. “I note the inquiry continues its important work, and we are months away from findings and conclusions. “I will forever remain grateful for the opportunity to serve, and hope I have made some positive contributions along the way.” Multiple people advised the school funding organisation to allow McInerney to resign, but the board decided to terminate his contract.



Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Former minister on verge of tears over sacking, realisation she was ‘used’ by a friend In a statement, Catholic Schools NSW said the ICAC inquiry was of “deep concern” to the organisation and its stakeholders. “The board will work constructively … to ensure there is an externally conducted review of [our] operations,” the statement said. The organisation did not respond to questions about whether the review would be made public. Michael Bezzina, who has been a director of Catholic schools in both the Sydney and Parramatta dioceses and now works as a consultant, said the allegations aired in ICAC had cast a shadow over the sector but McInerney’s sacking meant there was now a chance for a reset. “I took from the communique from Catholic Schools NSW that there is a strong resolve to learn lessons from what has emerged during this terrible situation,” Bezzina said.



“Knowing the board chair as I do, I know she will certainly be pushing the board to make sure it learns from this.“ Independent Education Union of Australia NSW/ACT branch secretary Carol Matthews said she was not surprised by the termination. “It is vital that government funding of non-government schools is used solely for the purpose for which it is intended,” Matthews said. “The community must have confidence that public money is being used for educating school students and not for improper purposes.“ She said NSW law required “very close scrutiny of expenditure at the school level” to ensure funding was used for the benefit of students and the operation of schools.



“However, the legislation needs to be expanded to apply the same scrutiny to the bodies that receive funding on behalf of non-government schools,” she said. Investigators claim up to $265,000 in schools funding was diverted to two companies, Beckington and JPG Advisory, via sham invoices. Beckington was run by Christian Ellis, a key figure behind the Reformers, as well as lobbyist and former political staffer Jeremy Greenwood. The ICAC says Beckington and JPG did little or no work for Catholic Schools NSW, and the monthly retainers and sign-on fees were instead used to prop up the work of the Reformers. The ICAC argues funding for the group between 2019 and 2023 ultimately benefited the Liberal Party and therefore constitutes a political donation. McInerney has repeatedly denied knowledge of such a scheme. Catholic Schools NSW was formed in 2016 to replace the Catholic Education Commission after bishops at the time expressed a desire for a more “appropriate, efficient and transparent” administration.



Senior counsel for the commission Dr Peggy Dwyer. Sam Mooy McInerney’s role as a Liberal Party powerbroker was well known to the Catholic Schools NSW board as well as the Catholic Church and Archbishop Anthony Fisher. McInerney was on Wednesday accused of destroying evidence that could be relevant to the ICAC’s Operation Rosny inquiry – a claim he denied. The senior counsel leading the watchdog’s case against a group of conservative Liberal Party operatives was left dumbstruck when McInerney revealed he had performed a factory reset on his iPhone and iPad over the weekend while still sworn in as a witness. McInerney claimed he erased everything on his phone because the National Australia Bank had placed a block on his main spending account due to a suspicious overseas transaction.



David Elliott speaks to the media after his ICAC appearance. Peter Rae Elliott, the former cabinet minister, told the ICAC on Friday that the developer Nassif “went nuts” after Elliott campaigned against development in his electorate. He said he was then tailed by private investigators, subjected to death threats and confronted by Nassif on two occasions. In the first approach, Elliott said Nassif confronted him at Castle Towers and demanded to speak to him about his developments. Elliott said he told Nassif he didn’t speak to property developers. Nassif then made another approach to Elliott at a pub in Parramatta, where he told the MP he wanted to introduce him to his daughter, and again demanded to speak with Elliott about development. Elliott says he refused.



Elliott said his chief of staff, Tanya Raffoul, was “threatened” by Nassif multiple times through the Lebanese community. Raffoul went to the same church as Nassif. In one instance Raffoul was called into a meeting with Nassif, who claimed to have photos of Elliott. Elliott told the ICAC Nassif said words to the effect of “you’re going to have to spill your guts on him [Elliott] and we’re going to need you to resign and essentially turn on him, and that you know his career would be ending the next day”. Elliott said he became aware there were negative stories about him being briefed to journalists while he was a government minister. He said he formed the view Nassif was behind the campaign because “he had left a message on my mobile that he was going to get me”. The inquiry continues next week.

World.title: ASX slides for second week amid sell-off in local banks
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides for second week amid sell-off in local banks Adrian Black Updated August 21, 2026 — 5:28pm ,first published August 21, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian shares have fallen for a second week amid high oil prices, US bond market concerns and a sell-off in local banks as housing market gloom persists. The S&P/ASX200 fell 24.9 points on Friday, down 0.27 per cent, to 9,058.9, as the broader All Ordinaries lost 28.8 points, or 0.31 per cent, to 9269.7. Wall Street closed in the red for the fourth time in five days. Bloomberg The top 200 has dropped almost 2.5 per cent since resetting record highs earlier in August after housing market concerns sparked a banking sell-off that has loomed large over earnings season. Energy and gold stocks offered some support as oil prices climbed and historically high US debt and Treasury yields rattled investors, prompting the US government to intervene in its roughly $US60 trillion ($A84 trillion) bond market.



The move was concerning and echoed interventions that preceded 1992’s Black Wednesday pound crisis and 2015’s Swiss Franc shock, Moomoo market strategist Michael McCarthy said. “It appears that we regularly need to repeat the lesson that nobody is bigger than the market,” he said. “In both of those cases, the governors of the Bank of England and the Swiss National Bank tried to hold back the tide, and eventually they got washed away by it. “What happened this week has increased the likelihood that the next financial crisis will originate in the US bond market.” Caution was the order of the day, with investors taking profits on a recent rally in healthcare stocks, while consumer spending housing market concerns continued to weigh on discretionary retail (down 1.8 per cent) and property stocks (down 2.4 per cent).



The heavyweight financials sector inched 0.2 per cent higher but has dived more than eight per cent in two weeks after major banks reported home loan applications have plummeted since May’s federal budget. Related Article Opinion

GST The GST carve-up is cooked, but we need to stop piling onto WA Millie Muroi Economics Writer Resources advanced have gained 5.5 per cent since Monday, while gold stocks surged for a third straight week, further bolstered by US debt concerns that downgraded the greenback’s safe-haven status. The energy sector has advanced for seven of the past eight weeks, tracking with a resurgent oil price after the US threatened to broaden sanctions on Iran and its trading partners. Local earnings season is in full swing, helping TPG Telecom, Guzman y Gomez, and Regis Resources shares rise on the backs of solid results.



On the flip side, Charter Hall, Perpetual, GQG, ARN Media and Inghams tumbled after their financials failed to impress. The Australian dollar is buying 71.46 US cents, up from 71.22 US cents on Thursday. Cryptocurrency bitcoin has had its best week in almost a year, surging almost 20 per cent to $US75,400 ($A105,550) after US President Donald Trump called on Congress to pass a crypto regulation bill. Overnight on Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 0.9 per cent for its fourth loss in the five days since setting its record last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1 per cent. The bond market remains the centre of the action after yields charged higher through the northern summer on worries about high inflation, gargantuan government debts and other factors. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent made a move that jolted financial markets to at least double the size of his department’s planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 to November 4.



Related Article Analysis

Trump's America Trump’s America faces a ‘doom loop’ as it falls in a $56 trillion hole That helped to push yields down after the 10-year Treasury’s yield had hit its highest level in more than a year, and the 30-year yield got back to where it was in 2007, before the Great Recession sent yields towards zero worldwide. It’s a big deal because high yields slow the economy by raising interest payments for people, companies and the government, and they can undercut prices for shares and other investments. But analysts had cautioned the effect may be short-lived, given how small the purchases are relative to the overall size of the Treasury market and how they don’t fix the fundamental concerns of investors that had driven up yields in the first place. Plus, more signals arrived quickly to push worries higher. The US government’s debt topped $US40 trillion ($56.2 trillion) on Wednesday, a staggering record that arrived months after the national debt first blew past the $US39 trillion mark in April, because Washington continues to spend far more money than it brings in.
